lens: Production-ready modern web platform features (Baseline 2024-2026 plus progressive enhancements) for Detent's premium marketing and commerce site: current browser support as of 2026-09-26, the fallback for each feature, and where it goes on Detent. Researched from web.dev monthly platform posts (Jan-Aug 2026), WebKit's Safari 27.0 notes (shipped Sept 17, 2026), MDN Firefox 150-156 release notes, the Interop 2026 announcements, Chrome developer blogs and 2026 practitioner write-ups. Current stable versions: Chrome 152 (Aug 2026, the latest the monthly posts cover), Firefox 156 (Sept 15, 2026), Safari 27.0 (Sept 17, 2026). Each finding says whether it is proven practice or an emerging bet.

findings.title: Use native cross-document View Transitions as the site's page transitions, not Astro ClientRouter or any SPA router
findings.detail: PROVEN in 2 of 3 engines, and a safe bet for the next decade (it is in Interop 2026, which now covers cross-document transitions). Support: same-document transitions have been Baseline since Oct 14, 2025 (Firefox 144). :active-view-transition has been Baseline since Jan 13, 2026. Cross-document transitions work in Chromium 126+ and Safari 18.2+. Firefox 156 still has not shipped them, so Firefox users get a normal navigation, which is the correct fallback. Recipe: put `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference){ @view-transition { navigation: auto; } }` in the shared layout (both pages must opt in, and it only runs on same-origin, user-initiated, non-POST navigations). Give the dial a stable name, e.g. `.dial-stage{view-transition-name: dial}`, and repeat it on home, PDP, /configure and /for/* so the knob appears to fly between pages. Names must be unique per page. Use `view-transition-class` to style groups of elements together, and `view-transition-name: match-element` for lists of cards. For direction, set types from the lifecycle events: in `pagereveal` read `navigation.activation.from` and `.entry` (Navigation API, Baseline Jan 2026), then call `e.viewTransition.types.add('forward'|'back'|'zoom-in')`, and style with `html:active-view-transition-type(zoom-in)`. In `pageswap`, set names only on the element being navigated to (e.g. the feel-profile card that was clicked). There is a hard 4-second timeout: if the new page is not renderable in 4s the transition is dropped, so treat 4s as a performance budget. Use `<link rel="expect" href="#hero" blocking="render">` (Chromium) so the named element exists at first paint. Add `object-fit: cover` on `::view-transition-old/new(dial)` so bitmap snapshots don't stretch. Always guard with `if (!e.viewTransition) return;`.
findings.applyTo: BaseLayout.astro (global @view-transition rule plus pageswap/pagereveal module). Named elements: dial stage (home <-> PDP <-> /configure <-> /for/*), product finish swatch -> configurator, feel-profile card -> /feels/[slug], integration logo -> /integrations/[app]. Types: 'forward' for tease->waitlist->reserve funnel steps, 'back' for history traversal, 'zoom-in' for grid->detail.
findings.risk: No cross-document support in Firefox as of 156, so never make meaning depend on the animation. A three.js <canvas> snapshot can come out blank or stale on the old page (WebGL preserveDrawingBuffer:false), so in pageswap render one final frame or put the name on a wrapper whose static AVIF poster is swapped in. Don't put view-transition-name on elements under content-visibility:auto. Long animations hurt INP-sensitive flows, so keep them to about 250-400ms. Honour reduced motion.

findings.title: Speculation Rules for near-instant funnel navigation, gated so three.js, audio and analytics wait for page activation
findings.detail: PROVEN in Chromium (about 70%+ of traffic). Safari 26.2 has an implementation that is off by default, and Firefox has none. GitHub Pages cannot send a Speculation-Rules header, so use an inline `<script type="speculationrules">`. Recommended config: {"prerender":[{"where":{"and":[{"href_matches":"/*"},{"not":{"href_matches":["/reserve/*","/checkout*","/*?*ref=*"]}},{"not":{"selector_matches":"[data-no-prerender]"}}]},"eagerness":"moderate"}],"prefetch":[{"urls":["/waitlist/"],"eagerness":"eager"}]}. The prefetch URL should change per launch phase: on /tease prefetch the next funnel page. Chrome eagerness: moderate fires on about 200ms hover or pointerdown on desktop. On mobile it uses viewport heuristics: links within 30% vertical distance of the last pointerdown, at least 0.5x the largest anchor, 500ms after scrolling stops. Limits: immediate/eager allow 50 prefetches and 10 prerenders; moderate/conservative keep 2, first-in-first-out. Measured impact (Shopify): median desktop -285ms TTFB, -224ms FCP, -228ms LCP, about 10% of navigations at 0ms TTFB, but only about 25ms on mobile. Critical gate: prerendered pages run JS, so wrap heavy or side-effecting init with `if (document.prerendering) document.addEventListener('prerenderingchange', init, {once:true}); else init();`. That covers the WebGPU adapter request, the AudioContext, analytics pageview and referral-code attribution. Prerendering also lets cross-document view transitions start instantly, well inside the 4s budget.
findings.applyTo: BaseLayout.astro inline rules, with the rules object generated from the launch-phase config so each phase prefetches its next step. Exclude reservation/deposit, Stripe/checkout, referral-claim and any URL that mutates state. Put the prerendering gate in the shared analytics module, the <detent-dial> bootstrap and the audio engine.
findings.risk: Chromium-only today, so treat it purely as an enhancement. Prerendering a page with side effects double-counts analytics and referral credits. Prerenders cost bandwidth, so don't prerender while navigator.connection.saveData is on (Chromium). The 'eager' semantics were redefined in 2025, so test in DevTools > Application > Speculative loads.

findings.title: Scroll-driven animations (animation-timeline) for the teardown story, and CSS scroll-triggered animations as an emerging bet for reveals
findings.detail: Support: Chrome 115+ and Safari 26+ (two engines, about 84% global by mid-2026). Firefox has scroll-driven animations fully implemented but still behind `layout.css.scroll-driven-animations.enabled` in release (on in Nightly). The feature is part of Interop 2026 and the supporting pieces keep landing: animation-range in 150/151, timeline-range-name in @keyframes in 152, view-timeline-inset in 155. Expect it to be on by default soon. Recipe: `.part{ animation: explode linear both; animation-timeline: view(); animation-range: contain 0% contain 100%; }`. The `animation-timeline` declaration must come AFTER the `animation` shorthand, because the shorthand resets it. Fallback trick: don't set a duration in the shorthand, so browsers without support snap to the end state (content visible) instead of animating on load. Wrap everything in `@supports (animation-timeline: view()) and (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)`. For the three.js hero, don't read CSS every frame. Use the JS `ScrollTimeline`/`ViewTimeline` objects' `currentTime` where available, or a passive scroll listener feeding a rAF loop. Emerging: scroll-triggered animations (Chrome 145/146), which play a time-based animation once a threshold is crossed: `timeline-trigger: --t view() contain 15% contain 85% / entry 100% exit 0%; animation-trigger: --t play-forwards play-backwards;`. Fallback is IntersectionObserver toggling a class. It will likely win because the browser can run it off the main thread, replacing the most common GSAP/IntersectionObserver use.
findings.applyTo: PDP 'Inside Detent One' exploded view: CNC body, BLDC gimbal motor, 14-bit magnetic encoder and 1.28-inch round display separate as you scroll, using view() with animation-range. Reading-progress hairline on long pages using scroll(root). Knurling texture parallax. Spec-table reveals and feel-profile card entrances via scroll-triggered animations with an IntersectionObserver fallback. The hero dial's idle rotation and scroll coupling handled in JS from the same scroll progress.
findings.risk: Firefox release still lacks it, so layouts must read fine in the static end state. Never scroll-jack. Test for jank when three.js and CSS scroll animations run at the same time on low-end Android. `animation-range` names differ subtly across engines, so run WPT-style checks in Safari 26/27. Scroll-triggered animations are Chromium-only.

findings.title: Replace modal, drawer and tooltip JavaScript with Popover API, <dialog> and invoker commands (command/commandfor), with closedby and popover=hint as enhancements
findings.detail: Support: the Popover API has been Baseline since 2024. Invoker commands became Baseline in Dec 2025 (Chrome 135, Firefox 144 on Oct 14 2025, Safari 26.2 on Dec 12 2025). The :open pseudo-class became Baseline in May 2026 (Safari 26.5). Declarative wiring: `<button commandfor="cart" command="show-modal">`, `<button commandfor="sound-settings" command="toggle-popover">`. The built-in commands are show-modal, close, request-close, toggle-popover, show-popover and hide-popover. Custom commands must start with `--` and fire a `command` event on the target web component, e.g. `<button commandfor="dial" command="--snap-to-12">` with `dial.addEventListener('command', e => e.command === '--snap-to-12' && ...)`. That makes every feel-profile preset button zero-JS glue. `closedby="any"` (light dismiss for dialogs) is in Chrome 134 and Firefox 141 but not in stable Safari (only Safari Technology Preview 249, July 2026). Fallback: `dialog.addEventListener('click', e => { if (e.target === dialog) dialog.close(); })`. `popover="hint"` (Chrome 133; Safari TP 249) opens tooltips without closing an open auto popover. Unknown popover values fall back to 'manual' behaviour, so hints just lose light-dismiss. `interestfor` hover/long-press invokers are Chrome 142 only, so use the mfreed7/interestfor polyfill or open on click.
findings.applyTo: Cart drawer (<dialog> with show-modal), the sound and haptics settings popover in the nav, the 'What's a detent?' glossary hints, integration hover cards on /integrations (interestfor with click fallback), feel-profile preset buttons that talk to <detent-dial> via --custom commands, the reservation terms dialog, and the referral share sheet.
findings.risk: Keep a small invokers polyfill (keithamus/invokers-polyfill) only for iOS below 26.2 and old Chromium, loaded behind `if (!('command' in HTMLButtonElement.prototype))`. The closedby, popover=hint and interestfor attributes must be enhancements, not dependencies. Test focus return and inert background in all three engines.

findings.title: CSS anchor positioning for product hotspots, tooltips and the mini-cart: use the core, and feature-query the newer sub-features
findings.detail: Baseline Newly available in Jan 2026 when Firefox 147 shipped it (Chrome 125, Safari 26). The spec is still being refined through Interop 2026: Safari 27 added transform-aware anchoring, changed the `position-anchor` default to `normal`, and renamed `position-visibility` keywords to `anchor-valid`/`anchor-visible`. The web-features data now lists the very latest versions (Chrome/Firefox 151, Safari 27) for the full feature set, so treat the core as stable and the extras as progressive. Recipe: `.hotspot{anchor-name: --encoder}` and `.tip{position: absolute; position-anchor: --encoder; position-area: top; position-try-fallbacks: flip-block, flip-inline; margin: unset;}`, combined with `popover="hint"`. Note the `margin: unset` for anchored popovers, because the CSSWG disables auto margins when position-area is set, and older implementations differ. For the 3D hotspots, project the vertex positions to screen space in the three.js loop and write them to `--x/--y` on invisible anchor <span>s. The CSS then places the tooltip, and Safari 27 follows transforms correctly.
findings.applyTo: PDP 3D hotspots labelling the machined parts (encoder, BLDC motor, display, USB-C), spec-term tooltips, the configurator swatch hover labels, the nav mini-cart anchored to the cart icon, and the feel-library 'try this feel' callouts.
findings.risk: There are cross-engine differences in how position-area shifts overflowing boxes (Chrome only shifts on the block axis), so test at 320px width. In `@supports not (anchor-name: --a)`, fall back to centred popovers, or lazy-load Floating UI only there. Don't depend on anchor-size() or position-visibility.

findings.title: Entry and exit motion without JS: @starting-style, transition-behavior: allow-discrete, exclusive <details name>, ::details-content, and interpolate-size as a Chromium enhancement
findings.detail: Baseline 2024: @starting-style, `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` and exclusive accordions via `<details name="faq">` (Chrome 120, Safari 17.2, Firefox 130). `interpolate-size: allow-keywords` and `calc-size()` are Chrome 129+ only; Firefox and Safari have positive standards positions but hadn't shipped as of 2026. Recipe for popovers: `[popover]{opacity:0; translate:0 8px; transition: opacity .2s, translate .2s, display .2s allow-discrete, overlay .2s allow-discrete} [popover]:popover-open{opacity:1; translate:0; @starting-style{opacity:0; translate:0 8px}}`. Recipe for accordions: `:root{interpolate-size: allow-keywords}` and `details::details-content{block-size:0; overflow:clip; transition: block-size .3s, content-visibility .3s allow-discrete} details:open::details-content{block-size:auto}`. Where interpolate-size is missing the accordion just opens instantly, which is the right fallback. Use `calc-size(auto, size + 1rem)` only when the end size needs arithmetic.
findings.applyTo: FAQ and 'Is it worth $349?' objection-handling accordion (exclusive details name="faq"), spec-sheet groups, shipping/returns/warranty details in the reservation flow, cart drawer and popover entrances, and the feel-profile 'details' expanders in the library.
findings.risk: `overlay` in the transition list is Chromium-only (exit animations elsewhere are instant; fine). Check that find-in-page (auto-expanding details) still works. Keep durations at or under 300ms and remove motion under prefers-reduced-motion.

findings.title: Native form upgrades in the configurator and waitlist: customizable <select>, field-sizing, <input type=checkbox switch>
findings.detail: Customizable select (`appearance: base-select` on both `select` and `::picker(select)`, plus `::picker-icon`, `::checkmark`, `<selectedcontent>` and rich HTML inside <option>) shipped in Chrome 135 and Safari 27.0 (Sept 17, 2026). Firefox 153 changed the HTML parser to allow rich option content, and the feature itself is still behind `dom.select.customizable_select.enabled`. Unsupported browsers render a normal accessible select, with no JS fallback needed. `field-sizing: content` became Baseline Newly available in June 2026 (Firefox 152). The `<input type=checkbox switch>` renders as a native iOS toggle in Safari 17.4+ and as a plain checkbox elsewhere. UX guidance: for 3-4 finishes (Raw Aluminum, Anodized Graphite, Founders Brass), a visible radio-swatch group converts better than any select, because all options are seen and chosen in one tap. Use base-select for longer lists: 'Primary app' (Premiere, Resolve, Ableton, Figma, Blender, VS Code, OBS...) with app icons in options, knob-face display themes, region/plug.
findings.applyTo: /configure: finish swatches as radios; 'Map it to your app' uses a base-select with app icons whose `<selectedcontent>` mirrors the icon. Waitlist 'What would you control first?' textarea with `field-sizing: content; min-block-size: 3lh; max-block-size: 10lh`. Settings popover toggles for Sound and Haptics as `<input type=checkbox switch>`.
findings.risk: Firefox users (and anyone below Safari 27) see the native select. Design the unstyled state first. Don't nest interactive content inside options. The switch attribute is ignored in non-WebKit browsers, so style checkboxes with `appearance:none` as the base and let the switch be a WebKit bonus.

findings.title: Editorial-grade typography: text-wrap balance/pretty, text-box-trim (newly Baseline Aug 2026), and sibling-index() for procedural detent rings
findings.detail: `text-wrap: balance` is Baseline 2024; use it for h1-h3, headlines and CTAs. `text-wrap: pretty` is in Chrome 117+ and Safari 26+, with Firefox falling back to normal wrapping; use it on body copy and captions. `text-box: trim-both cap alphabetic` (text-box-trim and text-box-edge) became Baseline Newly available in Aug 2026 with Firefox 154 (Chrome 133, Safari 18.2). It removes the half-leading so display type and pill buttons are optically centred and headlines sit exactly on grid lines, the precision that premium, SOTD-level layouts show. `sibling-index()` and `sibling-count()` also became Baseline in Aug 2026 (Chrome 138, Safari 26.2, Firefox 154). Use them to draw the dial's tick ring with no JS, `.tick{rotate: calc((sibling-index() - 1) * 360deg / sibling-count())}`, and to stagger reveals with `animation-delay: calc(sibling-index() * 35ms)`. Fallback: Astro emits `style="--i:N; --n:M"` at build time and the CSS uses `var(--i)`. Upgrade to sibling-index() inside `@supports (rotate: calc(sibling-index() * 1deg))` for client-filtered lists where build-time indices go stale.
findings.applyTo: Global type scale (headings balance, body pretty, buttons text-box trim). The 12-click 'clock' ring and end-stop markers drawn around the CSS dial and fallback poster. Feel-library and integrations grid stagger. Launch countdown digits.
findings.risk: text-box-trim only became Baseline in Aug 2026, so older browsers show slightly more vertical padding. Design tolerances accordingly, not pixel-locked. Don't balance long paragraphs (performance cost).

findings.title: One color system for CSS and three.js: OKLCH, relative colors, color-mix(), light-dark(), contrast-color() and P3
findings.detail: All Baseline: OKLCH and color-mix() (2023), relative color syntax and light-dark() (2024), contrast-color() (Baseline Newly available April 2026 via Chrome 147; Firefox 146, Safari 26). Newer extras: multi-stop color-mix (Firefox 150, Safari 27), `alpha()` (Chrome 152, Safari 27) and light-dark() with images (Firefox 150, Safari 27). Tokens: `:root{color-scheme: light dark; --anodize-h: 255; --accent: oklch(0.72 0.14 var(--anodize-h)); --accent-hi: oklch(from var(--accent) calc(l + .08) c h); --surface: light-dark(oklch(.985 .003 255), oklch(.16 .012 255)); --hairline: color-mix(in oklch, currentColor 14%, transparent);}` and `@media (color-gamut: p3){ --accent: oklch(0.72 0.19 var(--anodize-h)); }` for richer anodized finishes on P3 screens. The configurator changes one hue/chroma token per finish, and everything (UI chrome, glows, the round display's UI) re-derives from it. Use `color: contrast-color(var(--finish))` for labels on swatches. Feed the same OKLCH value to the three.js material by converting it with a tiny OKLCH to linear-sRGB function (e.g. culori/fn), because THREE.Color.setStyle doesn't parse oklch().
findings.applyTo: tokens.css in @layer tokens. Finish-driven theming on /configure and PDP (the page recolors as you pick Graphite vs Brass). Dark-first theme with light-dark(). Per-audience accent hue on /for/editors, /for/producers, /for/designers, /for/developers and /for/streamers. Launch-phase accent shifts.
findings.risk: contrast-color() only returns black or white and only became Baseline in April 2026, so provide a fallback declaration first. Check contrast in both schemes with forced-colors on. Keep an sRGB fallback before P3 values.

findings.title: CSS architecture: @layer and native nesting, container queries (size, name-only, style), with scroll-state() and if() as Chromium-only enhancements; drive launch phases through data attributes and style queries
findings.detail: Baseline foundation: `@layer reset, tokens, base, layout, components, utilities, overrides;` plus native nesting (Baseline 2023), size container queries with cqi units, name-only container queries (Baseline May 2026, Chrome 148), and container style queries for custom properties (Baseline May 2026, Firefox 151). Launch-phase theming: the build writes `<html data-phase="reserve" style="--phase: reserve">` from the single launch config. Components switch with `[data-phase=reserve] &` or `@container style(--phase: live)`, so there are no runtime conditionals. Emerging and Chromium-only: `@container scroll-state(stuck: top)` (Chrome 133+; Safari 27 and Firefox have not shipped it, about 72% coverage) for a sticky Reserve bar that condenses and gains a hairline when stuck, and `scroll-state(snapped: x)` for the feel-profile carousel. Fallback: an IntersectionObserver sentinel toggling `data-stuck`. CSS `if()` is Chrome 137+ only (Safari TP 249 has it; Firefox in progress). Don't build core logic on it before Interop coverage. It will win eventually, because inline conditionals remove whole classes of modifier CSS.
findings.applyTo: Global stylesheet structure for Astro components and light-DOM web components (<detent-dial>, <feel-card>, <phase-cta>). The sticky buy/reserve bar on PDP and landing pages. /feels carousel. Audience landing pages reusing one component with different container widths.
findings.risk: Shadow DOM components don't inherit the page's layer order, so prefer light DOM plus @scope for most components. Style queries only work on custom properties cross-browser. scroll-state() and if() need @supports guards: `@supports (container-type: scroll-state)`.

findings.title: Haptics: navigator.vibrate works only on Android, and iOS 26.5 closed the programmatic switch trick, so design haptics as a single-tick, direct-tap bonus
findings.detail: Facts as of Sept 2026: the Vibration API works in Chromium and Firefox on Android (it needs sticky user activation) and has never shipped in WebKit, so no iOS browser has it. The trick of calling `.click()` on the <label> of a hidden `<input type=checkbox switch>` triggered the Taptic Engine on iOS 17.4-26.4. iOS 26.5 patched the programmatic path, and all haptics libraries that scheduled repeated ticks broke. What still works on 26.5+: an invisible real switch overlaid on the tapped control, so the user's own trusted tap toggles it. That yields ONE tick per tap, and multi-pulse patterns only fire their first tick. Recipe: `const canVibrate = 'vibrate' in navigator;`. On Android detent crossings, fire `navigator.vibrate(10)` (8-15ms reads as a crisp tick; below about 8ms many actuators produce nothing), rate-limited to one pulse per 40ms during fast spins. Use `[12,40,12]` for end-stop bounces and `[25]` for a spring-return snap. On iOS, attach haptics only to discrete taps (preset buttons, '+1 detent' steppers, the Reserve button) through the overlay-switch pattern, and let Web Audio clicks carry the continuous drag. Put a Haptics switch in the settings popover (localStorage), default on, and label it honestly: 'Haptics (Android & supported iPhones)'.
findings.applyTo: <detent-dial> interaction layer (detent crossings, end-stops, spring-return), feel-profile 'try it' buttons, configurator steppers and the Reserve CTA confirmation tick. Copy on /feels should say 'Feel it on your phone (Android) and hear it everywhere', not promise iPhone haptics.
findings.risk: Apple may close the overlay path too, so never make comprehension depend on haptics. Vibration without prior user activation is silently blocked in Chrome. Excessive buzzing reads as cheap, so use short and sparse pulses. There is no prefers-reduced-haptics media query, so the settings toggle is required.

findings.title: Low-latency Web Audio detent clicks that respect the user's music and silent switch
findings.detail: Recipe: create one `new AudioContext({latencyHint: 'interactive'})` lazily on the first `pointerdown`, not click or pointerup (it fires earlier and counts as activation). At that point, pre-render every feel's click and ratchet sample once with an OfflineAudioContext: a filtered noise burst of about 3-6ms plus a resonant body of about 1.2-4kHz shaped by the feel profile. Store them as AudioBuffers in a Map, and on each detent crossing start a one-shot AudioBufferSourceNode through a shared GainNode. Don't build oscillator graphs per tick, and cap voices at 1 per 12ms. Above that rate, crossfade into a pre-rendered continuous ratchet loop whose playbackRate tracks angular velocity. Read `ctx.outputLatency` (broadly available since March 2025): if it is over about 0.08s (typical of Bluetooth earbuds), soften the clicks and show 'Bluetooth audio adds lag. Use speakers or wired audio for the true feel'. iOS: Safari puts a bare AudioContext in the 'ambient' session, which mixes with the user's music and obeys the silent switch. Keep that default for UI clicks. Setting `navigator.audioSession.type = 'playback'` (Safari 16.4+; it must be set BEFORE the AudioContext is created) would pause a producer's Spotify and override silent mode, which is hostile for UI sound. When sound is on, show a one-line hint on iOS: 'On silent? Flip the switch to hear the detents'. Sound defaults to off until the first dial interaction, which shows a small 'Sound on?' chip. Suspend the context on `pagehide` and resume on `pageshow` so the page can enter the back/forward cache (bfcache).
findings.applyTo: src/lib/audio/detent-engine.ts shared by the hero dial, /feels library previews (each profile has its own synthesized click), the configurator 'listen to the finish' easter egg (brass vs aluminum timbre) and the launch-day countdown ticks.
findings.risk: Autoplay policies mean nothing plays before a user gesture. Synthesized clicks can alias at 44.1kHz vs 48kHz, so render at `ctx.sampleRate`. Sound must never be required: provide captions and visual tick flashes. Test with iOS silent mode on/off and with background music playing.

findings.title: three.js WebGPURenderer with automatic WebGL2 fallback: write shaders in TSL from day one, and never let the canvas become the LCP element or block input
findings.detail: WebGPU now ships by default in Chrome/Edge (desktop plus Android 12+), Safari 26 on macOS, iOS, iPadOS and visionOS, Firefox 141 on Windows and Firefox 145 on Apple Silicon macOS. Firefox on Linux, Android and Intel Macs is still pending, and global coverage is about 87% (Sept 2026). three.js r171+ `import * as THREE from 'three/webgpu'` falls back to WebGL2 automatically; the current release is r186. Checklist: `await renderer.init()` before render(), because r186 throws otherwise. Detect the backend with `renderer.backend.isWebGPUBackend`, not isWebGPURenderer. Support a `?webgl` flag via `new WebGPURenderer({forceWebGL})` for QA. Run `await renderer.compileAsync(scene, camera)` before revealing, to avoid first-frame shader stalls. Use RenderPipeline (not EffectComposer) and TSL node materials, because ShaderMaterial, RawShaderMaterial and onBeforeCompile are unsupported on BOTH backends. Import only three/webgpu, since mixing in `three` grew one bundle from 792KB to 1155KB. Cap DPR with `Math.min(devicePixelRatio, 2)` (1.5 on mobile or low core counts). Render on demand (only while the dial moves or an animation runs) and pause via IntersectionObserver and `visibilitychange`. That keeps the premium feel without draining battery or starving INP. LCP strategy: the hero ships an AVIF poster `` of the exact first frame. three.js is dynamically imported after load, during idle time, and cross-fades in once compileAsync resolves. Why WebGPU is the 10-year bet: compute shaders (e.g. an anisotropic brushed-aluminum shader, spark particles on end-stop hits) and it's the API every engine is investing in; WebGL2 remains the fallback.
findings.applyTo: <detent-dial-3d> hero on home, PDP, audience pages and /configure (finish, knob-face theme and display UI rendered live). Low-power mode (reduced motion, Save-Data, `navigator.hardwareConcurrency <= 4`, or a failed init) shows the poster plus the CSS dial, keeping interaction fully functional.
findings.risk: TSL porting is the real cost. A WebGL2 fallback leak was reported (three.js issue #34597: programs, shaders and VAOs not deleted), so test long sessions on the fallback path. The canvas snapshot in view transitions needs care. Test real devices: iPhone 12-era, mid-range Android, Firefox/Linux (WebGL2 path). Prerendered pages must not request an adapter until activation.

findings.title: 'See it on your desk': Safari 27's <model> element and AR Quick Look (emerging bet)
findings.detail: Safari 27.0 (Sept 17, 2026) brought the HTML `` element to iOS, iPadOS and macOS (previously visionOS only) for native, GPU-efficient USDZ rendering with drag-to-rotate. It supports `environmentmap`/`stagemode` attributes and the `dynamic-range-limit` CSS property for HDR, and on visionOS it can drive immersive website environments. It is Apple-only for now. Recipe: `` (fallback content renders elsewhere), plus a proven AR Quick Look link `` for iPhone users to place the dial on their real desk at 1:1 scale. Use Android Scene Viewer or with a GLB when a user explicitly asks for AR. It will likely matter over the decade because spatial platforms (visionOS and future Android XR) favour declarative 3D over canvas code, and 'at true size on your desk' shows scale honestly, which justifies a $349 price.
findings.applyTo: PDP and /configure: a 'View on your desk' button (AR Quick Look on iOS; hidden where unsupported). The <model> element as a zero-JS alternative for the per-finish viewer on Safari 27. Export USDZ and GLB per finish from the same source model in the asset pipeline.
findings.risk: Apple-only today, so it must be an add-on to the three.js experience, not a replacement. Asset budget: keep USDZ under about 4-6MB per finish, and lazy-load. Feature-detect with `'HTMLModelElement' in window`.

findings.title: Navigation API for shareable configurator state and direction-aware transitions
findings.detail: Baseline Newly available in Jan 2026 (Chrome 102, Firefox 147, Safari 26.2). Safari 26.2 lacks `precommitHandler`, which is an Interop 2026 item. Uses on a static site: (1) Configurator state lives in the URL (`/configure/?finish=graphite&face=clock&feel=ratchet24`) and is updated with `navigation.navigate(url, {history: 'replace', state})` while scrubbing, then pushed on commit, so every build is deep-linkable and shareable and Back works as expected. (2) Same-document filtering in /feels and /integrations: `navigation.addEventListener('navigate', e => { if (!e.canIntercept || e.hashChange || e.downloadRequest) return; if (sameRoute(e.destination.url)) e.intercept({ handler: () => document.startViewTransition(() => render(e.destination.url)).finished }); })`. (3) In cross-document `pagereveal`, `navigation.activation.navigationType === 'traverse'` together with `activation.from` indices decides the 'back' vs 'forward' view-transition type.
findings.applyTo: /configure state syncing, /feels and /integrations filter and sort (same-document, URL-driven), the funnel step direction for transitions, and restoring the referral code (`?ref=`) into state without extra history entries.
findings.risk: Keep a tiny History API fallback for Safari below 26.2 and older browsers. Don't intercept cross-page navigations: the site stays a true multi-page app so it keeps bfcache, speculation rules and native cross-document view transitions.

findings.title: Viral loop plumbing: Web Share Level 2 with a pre-generated 'My Detent' image card and a clipboard fallback
findings.detail: `navigator.share({files, title, text, url})` with `navigator.canShare({files})` works in Safari on iOS and macOS and in Chromium on Android and desktop. Firefox desktop has basic share only behind a preference and no file sharing, and desktop Web Share is still being made testable (a proposed Interop 2027 investigation). Key detail: share() needs transient activation, and awaiting `canvas.toBlob()` inside the click can lose it in Safari. So PRE-GENERATE the file whenever the build changes: render a 1080x1350 card from the three.js canvas plus an overlaid OffscreenCanvas with the finish name, the feel profile, 'Founder #0421' and the referral URL, cache it as a `File('detent-build.png', {type:'image/png'})`, then call share synchronously in the click. Fallback chain: canShare(files) -> share(files); else share({url, text}); else `navigator.clipboard.write([new ClipboardItem({'image/png': blob})])` plus copy link; else `<a download>`. The copy pattern is a prefilled line with the referral link that moves you up the waitlist, e.g. 'I just built my Detent One: Graphite, 24-detent ratchet. Skip the line:'.
findings.applyTo: Waitlist confirmation ('Move up the line' share), /configure 'Share your build', feel-profile pages ('Share this feel'), and the launch-day reservation confirmation. Every share URL carries ?ref= plus UTM, and the referral credit is applied only after activation, never in prerender.
findings.risk: The share sheet dismissal rejects with AbortError, which must not be treated as an error in analytics. Firefox desktop users get the clipboard path. Keep the card under about 1-2MB. Test on iOS with a user gesture from a <button>, not a pointerup on a canvas.

findings.title: GitHub Pages loading budget: fetchpriority, AVIF-first images, sizes="auto" (Baseline as of Safari 27), content-visibility, and a service worker, because you can't set headers or Early Hints
findings.detail: GitHub Pages serves a fixed `Cache-Control: max-age=600` and allows no custom headers. That means no 103 Early Hints, no Speculation-Rules, CSP, COOP or COEP headers, and no immutable caching. Mitigations: (1) Put `` on the hero poster (fetchpriority has been Baseline since Oct 2024), `` on the dial bootstrap only, and `fetchpriority="low"` plus dynamic import for three.js. (2) Images: AVIF first (Baseline since early 2024) with a JPEG/WebP fallback via Astro . Skip JPEG XL for now: Safari 17+ has partial support (no animation or progressive decoding), Chrome 145's jxl-rs decoder is flag-only, Firefox has it in Nightly only, and it is an Interop 2026 investigation area. (3) `sizes="auto"` for lazy images is now in Chrome 126, Firefox 150 and Safari 27, so use ``. (4) `content-visibility: auto; contain-intrinsic-size: auto 640px` on below-fold sections (Baseline since Sept 2024) for the long integrations directory, feel library, specs and FAQ. (5) A small service worker caches hashed `/_astro/*` assets forever, working around max-age=600. Use the Service Worker Static Routing API (Chromium 123+, Safari 27) so navigations go straight to the network: `e.addRoutes([{condition:{requestMode:'navigate'}, source:'network'}])`. (6) Put CSP in a . Optional: put Cloudflare in front of GitHub Pages later for Early Hints and real headers.
findings.applyTo: Astro image pipeline and BaseLayout head. The service worker registered after load (sw.js with static routes). Integrations directory, feel library and spec pages use content-visibility. The hero poster per finish is pre-rendered from the same 3D model so the poster-to-canvas swap is seamless.
findings.risk: Don't use content-visibility above the fold, on LCP elements, or on view-transition-named elements. A service worker adds startup cost to navigations unless static routing or navigation preload is used, and needs a versioned cleanup strategy. `sizes=auto` requires `loading=lazy` plus explicit width and height.

findings.title: Instant back/forward (bfcache) and fast interaction (INP): no unload listeners, close device and audio handles on pagehide, scheduler.yield in handlers, coalesced pointer input
findings.detail: LCP and INP became Baseline Newly available in Dec 2025 (Safari 26.2 added the Event Timing API), so real-user monitoring now covers all three engines. Safari's INP still has some over-reporting bugs. Targets: LCP under 2.0s at p75 mobile, INP under 100ms at p75 (the 'good' threshold is 200ms), CLS under 0.05. bfcache: never register `unload` (even an empty handler blocks bfcache) and use pagehide instead. Close Web Serial/HID ports and suspend AudioContext and render loops on `pagehide`, and resume on `pageshow` when `e.persisted`. Chrome 149 now lets pages with WebSockets into bfcache (their connections are closed), and GitHub Pages sends no `no-store`. Log `performance.getEntriesByType('navigation')[0].notRestoredReasons` on back_forward navigations. The Reserve -> PDP -> Reserve comparison loop must be instant. INP: the dial's pointermove handler does only immediate feedback (set `--angle` on the element, play the click, one vibrate) and batches the rest. Use `e.getCoalescedEvents()` for precise 14-bit-feeling tracking, `touch-action: none` on the dial, and rAF-coalesced rendering. Heavy follow-up work (material swaps, localStorage, analytics) goes after `await (globalThis.scheduler?.yield?.() ?? new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0)))`. scheduler.yield is in Chrome 129+ and Firefox (whose 156 release refined its priority inheritance), but not Safari.
findings.applyTo: Shared lifecycle module used by <detent-dial>, the audio engine, the three.js renderer and the optional device connector. Real-user monitoring beacon (web-vitals attribution build) posting to a lightweight endpoint. Performance budgets enforced in CI (Lighthouse CI) against the tease, waitlist, PDP and configure templates.
findings.risk: 'masked' notRestoredReasons hide third-party causes, so audit any embeds (video, chat, payment iframes) on funnel pages. A long three.js shader compile can land inside an interaction and wreck INP, so compile ahead of time with compileAsync during idle time.

findings.title: 'Plug it in to this page': browser-based device connect and firmware via Web Serial and WebHID (emerging bet; signals an open SDK and local-first product)
findings.detail: Web Serial now runs in desktop Chrome/Edge 89+, Chrome Android 148 and Firefox 151+ (May 2026). Firefox shows an add-on-gating explainer, then a port picker, and grants per site and per port. WebHID is Chromium desktop only. WebKit considers both harmful (fingerprinting), so Safari will not ship them. For Detent (an open-SDK, SmartKnob-inspired ESP32-class device), a no-install web configurator is the proven pattern from keyboard tools like VIA and Vial and esptool-js firmware flashers. Examples: 'Connect Detent' to live-push a feel profile from /feels to real hardware, update firmware, calibrate end-stops, and mirror the physical knob's angle into the 3D hero so the website turns when you turn the device. Before launch, show this as a 'Coming with your Detent' demo with a simulated device, and feature-detect `'serial' in navigator || 'hid' in navigator`. The payoff is marketing: a website you physically control is exactly the kind of moment people clip and share, and it makes the open-SDK claim tangible.
findings.applyTo: /feels/[slug] 'Send to my Detent' (post-launch), /setup (firmware and calibration), the developer landing page /for/developers (a live serial console demo), and a hidden easter egg on home: if a Detent is paired, the hero follows the real knob.
findings.risk: No Safari or iOS support, so every flow needs a desktop-companion or 'use Chrome/Firefox on desktop' path. Close ports on pagehide (bfcache). Requires a secure context (fine on GitHub Pages HTTPS). Firmware flashing needs a signed-image verification UX.

antiPatterns: Turning the multi-page Astro site into a single-page app (Astro ClientRouter, Barba, Swup) just to get page transitions. Native cross-document view transitions plus speculation rules do this now while keeping bfcache, crawlability and zero router JS.

Scroll-jacking or smooth-scroll libraries that hijack wheel and touch input (the Locomotive/Lenis-era Awwwards look). They hurt INP and accessibility and are no longer needed with native scroll-driven animations and scroll snap.
Making the WebGL/WebGPU <canvas> the LCP element, or importing three.js in <head>. Ship an AVIF poster of the first frame with fetchpriority=high, then lazy-load and cross-fade the renderer.
Writing new ShaderMaterial/GLSL or EffectComposer code for a WebGPURenderer project. It is unsupported on both backends, so write TSL and RenderPipeline from day one.
Rendering the 3D scene continuously at native DPR on 3x phones. Cap DPR at 1.5-2, render on demand, and pause offscreen and on hidden tabs.
Promising or relying on iPhone haptics. navigator.vibrate never shipped in WebKit, and iOS 26.5 killed programmatic switch-toggle haptics. Use haptics as an Android plus single-tap bonus only.
Setting navigator.audioSession.type='playback' for UI click sounds. It pauses the user's music and overrides the silent switch. Keep 'ambient' and ask for the switch to be flipped instead.
Autoplaying sound, or creating AudioContexts per click. Create one lazily on the first pointerdown and play pre-rendered buffers.
Prerendering or prefetching reservation, checkout or referral-claim URLs, or firing analytics and referral credits during prerender (check document.prerendering).
Registering unload handlers, leaving Web Serial/HID ports, audio or render loops open across navigation. Any of these silently kills instant back/forward.

Shipping Chromium-only features (scroll-state queries, CSS if(), interestfor, interpolate-size, scroll-triggered animations, speculation rules) as if they were Baseline, without @supports guards or a designed fallback state.
Keeping Floating UI/Popper, custom focus-trap modal libraries and JS accordions for things popover, dialog, invoker commands, anchor positioning and exclusive details now do natively.
Replacing a 3-option finish choice with a fancy dropdown because base-select exists. Visible swatches convert better, so use base-select for long lists only.
Betting on JPEG XL-only images, or pixel-perfect layouts that assume text-box-trim everywhere. Use AVIF-first with fallbacks and tolerant vertical rhythm.
Blanket content-visibility:auto on everything, including the hero, LCP or view-transition-named elements. It causes pop-in, broken snapshots and layout shift.
Assuming you can set HTTP headers on GitHub Pages (Early Hints, CSP, COOP/COEP, Cache-Control, Speculation-Rules). Design around meta tags, inline rules and a service worker, or front it with a CDN.

lens: Conversion-rate optimization for premium DTC hardware and creator tools, 2024-2026 and the next decade, applied to Detent One ($349 / Founders $399). Covers price justification, PDP and configurator UX, checkout friction, honest trust, social proof and urgency, the launch funnel (tease > waitlist > deposit > launch > store) with benchmarks per stage, email capture, alternatives to exit-intent popups, performance, and agentic commerce (JSON-LD, feeds, UCP/ACP, llms.txt). Research run on 2026-09-26: about 40 searches plus page fetches of Baymard, Stripe, Google Search Central, the FTC, web.dev, OpenAI commerce docs, the Google Developers blog and Adobe. Each finding says whether it is proven practice or an emerging bet. Numbers marked 'assumption' are internal targets with no public source behind them.

findings.title: Funnel benchmarks and instrumentation: a target for every stage of the launch-phase config
findings.detail:
PROVEN benchmarks, which become the pass/fail targets for each phase:
(1) TEASE page to waitlist signup: medians are 3.4% (SaaS), 4.1% (consumer apps) and 4.6% (AI tools); the top decile is above 8-9% (LaunchList). Detent target: 5% from cold paid traffic, 10-15% from warm social or referral traffic, because the interactive dial is the hook.
(2) Double opt-in verification: median 55-58%, top quartile above 70%. Target 70% or more by putting the confirm link behind a reward: 'confirm to lock your queue position'.
(3) Referral: median 9-10% of signups refer at least one person; strong programs exceed 18%. Target 15%, with k-factor 0.3-0.5. Assume nothing like Robinhood's roughly 3x.
(4) WAITLIST to paid deposit: 5-25%. It averages about 20% if you open deposits within 1 month of signup and falls below 10% after 3 months, because waitlists 'rot' (a16z speedrun). Waitlists convert 8-15% in general. Presale buyers later place 38% more orders and spend 34% more (Submarine, from $850M of orders). Target 15% of verified waitlisters inside the first 14 days of the deposit window.
(5) DEPOSIT landing visitors to reservation: strong preorder pages convert 10-20% of warm visitors. Target 8% blended.
(6) Deposit to balance paid at ship. Assumption, since no public benchmark exists: target 80% or more, and alert below 70%.
(7) LIVE STORE, electronics: sitewide conversion is 1.2-2.4% (Triple Whale 1.49%, other sources 1.9-2.41%). Target 2.5% or better, since single-SKU stores with strong hero pages beat catalog averages. Add-to-cart averages 6-8% (Dynamic Yield 6.08%); target 8%. Checkout completion is 45-55% for well-optimized stores (a Shopify sample median was 65%); target 60%. Cart abandonment averages 70.22% (Baymard); target below 60%.
(8) Email popups: Klaviyo median 2.3%, 'good' is 3-5%, exit-intent forms reach 10-13%.
(9) AI-referred sessions converted 31% better than other traffic in holiday 2025 (Adobe). Report them as their own channel.
findings.applyTo: src/config/launch.ts: each phase object carries {targets:{...}} beside its copy. An /ops/funnel debug overlay (dev only) and privacy-friendly analytics events: tease_view, dial_interact, waitlist_submit, email_verified, referral_share, deposit_start, deposit_paid, balance_captured, pdp_view, buy_click, express_pay_click, checkout_complete. Tag referrers from chatgpt.com, perplexity.ai, gemini.google.com and copilot as channel=ai.
findings.risk: Benchmarks mix SaaS and consumer data. Hardware-specific public data is thin, so treat these as starting targets and re-baseline after 2 weeks of real traffic. Cookieless analytics (Plausible, Fathom, or self-hosted Umami) avoids a consent banner and keeps the page light, but loses some attribution.

findings.title: Launch funnel: refundable deposit of about 14% of price, batch windows, and deposits opened within 30 days of the waitlist
findings.detail:
PROVEN pattern with 2024-26 evidence. Framework takes a fully refundable $100 deposit (10% of $999), sells in batches with later ship dates opening as each fills, and collects the balance only when the unit is ready to ship. Daylight DC-1 put a refundable $100 deposit checkbox (14% of $729) next to its free 'notify me' option. The deposit separates serious buyers from the curious and gives real demand data. Daylight's first 5,000-unit run sold out in days: more than 1,300 tablets and over $1M in the first 24 hours, $2.5M within days, and #1 on Hacker News. Rabbit r1 sold 3 batches of 10,000 in 4 days and reached over 100k preorders. Playdate sold 20,000 in about 17-20 minutes. Nothing Phone (1) used invites that expired after 48 hours, plus a £20 deposit.
DETENT MECHANICS: a $49 refundable deposit (14% of $349), credited in full to the order. Sell in Batches 1-N of 1,000 units, each with a stated ship window. The balance is charged only when the unit ships. Cancellation is one click, with an automated refund. Open deposits to the waitlist in referral-rank waves, each wave getting a 72-hour priority window that is honestly enforced server-side, then open to everyone. Open deposits no more than 30 days after the tease peak; after 3 months waitlist conversion falls below 10%.
Phase sequence in launch.ts: tease (dial demo plus email) > waitlist (queue position plus referral) > reserve (deposit, batch meter, Founders serial picker) > launch-day (live counter, press embeds, first-unboxing video) > store (express checkout, ship-by dates).
findings.applyTo: /launch/tease, /launch/waitlist, /launch/reserve, /launch/live and /shop are all driven by launch.ts {phase, batches:[{id, capacity, reserved, shipWindow}], depositAmount:4900, priorityWindowHours:72}. A <reserve-button> web component reads the phase and swaps its CTA: 'Join the list', then 'Reserve for $49 (fully refundable)', then 'Buy'.
findings.risk: A deposit is a paid preorder, so the FTC Mail/Internet Order Rule applies (see the deposit payments finding). Batch counts must come from the real database; a static site needs a tiny API such as a Cloudflare Worker or Supabase. In demo mode, label the counters as 'Demo data'. Never invent reservation numbers.

findings.title: Deposit payments and preorder law: use a captured, refundable charge (not an auth hold), and follow the FTC 30-day rule
findings.applyTo: Serverless endpoint (e.g. Cloudflare Worker /api/reserve) creates a Stripe Checkout Session or a PaymentIntent with setup_future_usage:'off_session' and metadata {batch, serial, finish}. /account/reservation has a one-click cancel that calls refunds.create. The delay-notice email template lives in the repo. The GitHub Pages site stays static; only /api/* runs elsewhere. Use Stripe test mode for the demo.
findings.risk: Refunded deposits still incur card fees on some processors, so budget for 3-4% leakage. Off-session balance charges can fail SCA in the EU/UK, so build a 'confirm your payment' email flow. Do not promise a ship date without supplier commitments behind it.

findings.title: Honest scarcity: numbered Founders serials, live batch meters and calendar ship dates in place of fake timers
findings.detail:
PROVEN: scarcity lifts conversion, and field studies show the effect is stronger for higher-priced items. But fake countdown timers, false hierarchies and drip pricing are named targets of the EU Digital Fairness Act, due to be proposed in late 2026, and FTC practice already treats them as deceptive.
EMERGING BET: make scarcity verifiable and personal.
(1) Founders Edition limited to a fixed run, e.g. 2,000 units numbered #0001-#2000 and laser-engraved on the underside. At reservation the buyer picks an available serial from a live grid; taken numbers show only the reserver's chosen display name, if they opted in. This is identity plus honest limit plus shareable artifact ('I got #0420').
(2) Batch meters built from real counts ('Batch 2 · 1,000 units · 812 reserved · ships by Mar 14 2027'), with a public changelog when a batch closes.
(3) A calendar ship date, never 'Q1'. Baymard finds 41% of sites fail to show a delivery date, and users misread 'business days'. Show 'Arrives Mar 17-20' and keep ranges within 5-7 days.
(4) An urgency end date only when it is real: 'Founders pricing ends when #2000 is reserved or on launch day, whichever comes first.'
findings.applyTo: <batch-meter> and <serial-picker> web components on /launch/reserve and the /shop Founders toggle. The serial grid is an accessible <fieldset> of radio buttons with aria-describedby status. The chosen serial is shown on the 3D dial's engraved underside (three.js decal) and rendered on the confirmation page's share card (OG image made with Satori at build, or the canvas-to-Web Share API at runtime).
findings.risk: Oversell race conditions: reserve the serial atomically server-side, with a 10-minute hold during checkout. If a batch slips, update the dates everywhere from launch.ts and email reservers, or you violate the FTC rule. Avoid any 'X people are viewing this' widget.

findings.title: Justifying the premium: no subscription, generous risk reversal and spec transparency, not decoy tricks
findings.detail:
(1) NO SUBSCRIPTION as the headline. Humane charged $699 plus $24 a month and saw returns outpace sales. Whoop's May 2025 upgrade-fee backlash showed how badly buyers react to recurring or clawed-back value. Detent is local-first with an open SDK, so say it plainly: 'Pay once. No account. No subscription. Works offline forever.'
(2) RISK REVERSAL. Baymard: 44% of sites hide the return policy from the PDP, 60% of users look for it there, and 13% abandon over an unsatisfactory policy. Offer a 100-day 'feel it' return window with free return shipping and a 3-year warranty, stated inline near the price.
(3) The DECOY EFFECT IS FRAGILE. Replications work in only about 12% of attempts (Yang & Lynn, 91 tries) and largely vanish with realistic stimuli (Frederick et al.). Don't invent a dummy third tier. Show two real editions (Standard $349, Founders $399), give Founders an honest 'Most reserved' label only once the data proves it, and make the default selection explicit.
(4) ANCHOR on the value of the workflow, not the price of rivals: 'Replaces a jog wheel, a MIDI encoder, and a macro pad.' If you show competitor prices, verify current street prices at publish time.
(5) COST-PER-USE belongs in secondary microcopy only. Gourville's 'pennies-a-day' framing reverses as the base price rises. Use '≈$0.30 per workday over 5 years' in a tooltip, backed by the warranty, and A/B test it rather than headlining it.
(6) MATERIALS STORY with numbers: 6061-T6 aluminum, CNC tolerances, 14-bit encoder = 16,384 positions per rev, detent torque range in mN·m, latency in ms. Show them in a three.js exploded view with an HTML spec table alongside.
findings.applyTo: /shop hero price block: price, BNPL line, a 'Pay once · no subscription' pill, and a returns and warranty row. /specs is a full HTML spec sheet. The /materials scroll story is an exploded GLB with the camera driven by the dial. Founders adds a numbered engraving, a machined walnut or brass base and a lifetime profile archive: a real product difference, not a decoy.
findings.risk: Once the 'no subscription' promise is published it must hold for the product's life. Put it in the versioned policy page (see the failures finding). A 100-day return window raises return reserves; budget 5-8% and use the returned units for refurbished sales.

findings.title: Product page and configurator UX: apply Baymard's 2025-26 pitfalls directly
findings.detail:
PROVEN (Baymard; only 48% of desktop and 38% of mobile sites score 'decent' or better on product pages):
(1) Button-style option selectors, never dropdowns (57% of sites get this wrong). Show finish and edition as large swatches, with sold-out states visible.
(2) In-scale imagery: 37% of sites lack it, and 42% of users try to judge size from images. Show the dial next to a hand, keyboard and mouse, with a '53 mm Ø × 38 mm' overlay, plus an AR link.
(3) Show the total cost on the page (67% of sites don't): 'Delivered by Mar 20 · $0 shipping · tax calculated at checkout (est. $28)'.
(4) The return policy summary inline (44% omit it).
(5) Save without an account (89% make saving hard). The configuration is serialized to the URL, and a 'Save build' action stores it with no login.
(6) Gifting on the PDP (78% omit it): 'Gift a reservation' with a claim-code email.
(7) Reviews: respond to negative ones (89% don't) and let visitors browse reviewer photos in place (63% can't).
(8) Mobile: a sticky buy bar with price and CTA (IntersectionObserver on the main CTA), swipeable gallery, tap targets of 44px or more.
EMERGING: the gallery's first slide is the live three.js model. Each finish change triggers a matching haptic 'click' (navigator.vibrate(8) on Android; iOS Safari doesn't support it) and a Web Audio detent sound.
findings.applyTo: /shop configurator: <finish-picker>, <edition-picker> and <delivery-estimate> components; URL state like ?finish=graphite&edition=founders&serial=0420, kept in sync via history.replaceState; 'View in your space' via <a rel="ar" href="/models/detent-one.usdz"> on iOS and a Scene Viewer intent on Android; sticky bar via position:sticky plus IntersectionObserver.
findings.risk: The WebGL gallery must not be the only representation: give it a static AVIF poster as the LCP element and alt text. The AR USDZ export needs its own pipeline. navigator.vibrate is unavailable on iOS, so haptics there are progressive enhancement only.

findings.title: Checkout: for the single hero SKU, skip the cart and put express wallets on the product page
findings.detail:
PROVEN:
- Showing Apple Pay to eligible users lifted conversion 22.3% and revenue 22.5% (Stripe, 50+ payment methods tested).
- Offering Apple Pay earlier in the flow via the Express Checkout Element roughly doubles conversion versus showing it only at the end.
- Adding at least one relevant payment method beyond cards gave +7.4% conversion and +12% revenue.
- Link has more than 200M users, up to +7% conversion for logged-in users and +14% for returning users.
- Shop Pay: up to +50% versus guest checkout (Shopify-commissioned study). As of June 2026 it is reportedly available off-Shopify via the Shop Pay Wallet API; verify before building.
- Baymard abandonment reasons: extra costs 40%, slow delivery 20%, card-security worries 19%, forced account creation 18-19%, long checkout 17%, total cost not visible upfront 12%. The average US checkout has 23.48 form elements; the ideal is 12-14 (7-8 fields). Better checkout design can lift conversion 35%.
For a single-SKU premium product, a cart page adds a step with no comparison value. A/B data on mobile cart drawers is mixed (-8% on one store), and high-ticket buyers want a full cost breakdown. So: Express Checkout Element buttons sit directly under 'Buy' on the product page, and 'Pay another way' opens a single-page guest checkout. Accessories (stand, spare knob faces) are offered as one-tap order bumps inside checkout, not upsell interstitials.
findings.applyTo: /shop: elements.create('expressCheckout', {buttonType:{applePay:'buy', googlePay:'buy', paypal:'buynow'}, buttonHeight:48, layout:{maxColumns:2, maxRows:1, overflow:'auto'}}); listen to 'availablepaymentmethodschange' to hide the empty container; use shippingaddresschange/shippingratechange to show a live delivery date. Register the domain for Apple Pay. /checkout: autocomplete tokens (given-name, family-name, email, address-line1, postal-code, cc-*), address autocomplete, 7-8 fields max, no forced account. A cart page exists only once more than one SKU is added.
findings.risk: Express wallets need a server (Checkout Sessions or PaymentIntents), so GitHub Pages alone can't process payments: use a Worker plus Stripe test mode for the demo, or Stripe Payment Links as a zero-backend fallback. Apple Pay requires domain verification on a custom domain (a github.io subdomain complicates this). Reading tax from the address sheet means 'est.' copy until it is confirmed.

findings.title: BNPL shown next to the price, not buried in checkout
findings.detail:
PROVEN directionally. Reported lifts come from providers and aggregators, so treat them as optimistic: conversion up to 21% higher on purchases of $250 or more, 20-30% overall, and AOV up 30-50%. Affirm's average order (about $255) suits $349-$399 tickets better than Klarna's (about $101). The Express Checkout Element supports Klarna as a button type ('pay'), and the Payment Element supports Affirm and Afterpay/Clearpay.
COPY PATTERN directly under the price, same font family, smaller size: '$349 or 4 interest-free payments of $87.25 · Klarna'. Only show amounts the provider will actually offer, using their messaging element (Stripe's Payment Method Messaging Element) so the numbers match the provider's terms.
findings.applyTo: /shop price block and the /launch/live sticky bar. Hide it in the deposit phase: a $49 deposit doesn't need financing. Show it in the store phase and for the balance-at-ship charge.
findings.risk: BNPL can read as 'discount-y' to premium buyers, so keep it visually quiet (text link, not a badge). The UK and EU are tightening BNPL advertising rules, so geo-gate the copy and use the provider's compliant messaging element instead of hand-written numbers.

findings.title: Accounts with passkeys, created after purchase and never before it
findings.detail: PROVEN plus EMERGING. Forced account creation causes 18-26% of abandonment (Baymard). FIDO Alliance's 2025 Passkey Index: passkey sign-in succeeds 93% of the time versus 63% for other methods, is 73% faster (8.5s vs 31.2s), and brands report about a 30% lift in conversion success. Pattern: guest checkout always. On the confirmation page: 'Track your Detent and manage your feel profiles: save a passkey (one tap).' That calls navigator.credentials.create({publicKey:{..., authenticatorSelection:{residentKey:'required', userVerification:'preferred'}}}). Returning users sign in through autofill: <input autocomplete="username webauthn"> plus navigator.credentials.get({mediation:'conditional'}). This works across Chrome, Safari and Firefox in 2026 and fits a local-first brand: no passwords stored.
findings.applyTo: /order/confirmed passkey upsell. /account (reservation, serial, cancel/refund, balance card update). The profile-library sync opt-in. The WebAuthn server lives in the same Worker as /api/* (e.g. SimpleWebAuthn).
findings.risk: Requires a backend and a relying-party ID on a stable custom domain; passkeys bound to *.github.io would break on migration. Provide an email magic-link fallback. Don't gate the free feel-profile library behind an account.

findings.title: Trust before reviews exist: open-source proof, unedited demos, a 'What it can't do' section, and a voluntary product passport
findings.detail:
Pre-launch there are no customer reviews, so build trust from verifiable artifacts.
(1) OPEN PROOF: link the SmartKnob lineage (Scott Bezek's open-source project) and show live GitHub stars and contributor counts for the Detent SDK, fetched at build plus refreshed client-side. Show the count of community feel profiles.
(2) UNEDITED DEMOS: a 60-second one-take video of real hardware with a visible latency readout. This answers the Rabbit/Humane problem, where polished demos outran reality.
(3) A 'What Detent One can't do (yet)' section. Candor raises credibility for premium, skeptical creator audiences, and it's cheap insurance against return-rate blowups.
(4) FOUNDER STORY with a named person and face (Daylight's founder-led mission story drove press and #1 on Hacker News).
(5) REPAIRABILITY: publish a teardown, screw types, a spare-parts price list (knob glass, bearing, cable) and firmware update guarantees ('Security and feature updates for 7 years, SDK forever open'). Framework proved repairability is a purchase driver.
(6) EMERGING BET: a voluntary Digital Product Passport page (QR on the box linking /passport/DT1-<serial>) with materials, origin, repair and recycling info. The EU ESPR requires DPPs for ICT products around 2029; shipping one now signals quality and future-proofs the brand.
findings.applyTo: /proof (or a homepage section) with <github-stats>, <build-log> and the demo video (AV1/H.264, poster, captions). /specs#limitations. /about/founder. /repair. /passport/[serial] (static template filled with demo data).
findings.risk: Live GitHub API calls hit rate limits (60/hr unauthenticated), so bake the numbers at build and refresh them in a scheduled GitHub Action. 'Can't do' copy needs discipline; don't turn it into humblebrag. The DPP is voluntary for now: don't claim regulatory compliance.

findings.title: Social proof without fakery: FTC Consumer Review Rule compliance, built into the components
findings.applyTo: <review-card> component with required props {verified:boolean, disclosure?:'free-unit'|'employee'|'affiliate'} that renders the disclosure badge automatically. <live-count> component requires a {source, asOf} prop and throws a build error if it gets a hard-coded number in production mode. Demo/concept mode shows a visible 'Concept demo: sample data' ribbon.
findings.risk: This is a concept site, so any sample reviews must be obviously labeled as illustrative, or omitted, to avoid appearing to fabricate testimonials. Prefer placeholders like 'Reviews open when Batch 1 ships.'

findings.title: Lessons from launch failures: public progress log, versioned policies, price lock and review units before balance capture
findings.detail:
PATTERNS drawn from 2024-26 hardware launches:
- RABBIT r1: more than 100k preorders and $20M, but a buggy device and 'why not just an app?' criticism destroyed word of mouth.
- HUMANE: $699 plus $24 a month, aimed at 100k units, sold about 10k, returns outpaced sales, and its assets went to HP for $116M against more than $230M raised.
- PLAYDATE: sold out in about 20 minutes, then a late battery defect pushed shipping into 2022.
- ANALOGUE 3D: sold out Oct 2024, slipped from Q1 to Jul, Aug and then Nov 2025, drew criticism for poor communication, and restocked $20 higher over tariffs.
- WHOOP: quietly changed a published free-upgrade promise, then reversed within days after screenshots spread.
DETENT RULES:
(1) A /progress build log with a dated monthly update, even if nothing changed ('EVT done, DVT in progress, next milestone: tooling T1').
(2) All promises (price lock for reservers, no-subscription, update lifetime, upgrade path) live on /policies as versioned Markdown with a visible changelog and git history link. Never silently edit.
(3) Price lock: 'Your $349 is locked, even if tariffs move the store price.'
(4) Put 20-50 production units with independent reviewers and creators before charging the Batch 1 balances, so buyers can cancel after reviews publish.
(5) Answer 'why hardware?' on the homepage: haptic force feedback can't be done on a phone or trackpad.
findings.applyTo: /progress (content collection of dated entries, RSS/Atom feed plus email digest), /policies (Astro content collection rendered from versioned MD with a git commit link), the launch.ts {priceLock:true} flag shown on reservation confirmation, and a homepage section 'Why this has to be a thing you touch'.
findings.risk: Public logs create accountability pressure; commit only to a cadence you can keep. Price lock is a real margin risk under tariff volatility, so price the deposit-phase MSRP with a buffer.

findings.title: Email capture: triggered by engagement, no discount, multi-step with segmentation
findings.detail:
PROVEN benchmarks:
- Klaviyo popup/flyout median submit rate 2.3%, goal of 3% or more; well-optimized forms reach 8-20%, and exit-intent forms 10-13%.
- Multi-step forms convert 5.64% vs 3.07% for single-step (84% higher). Caden Lane found that adding a context question increased conversion.
- Trigger after about 5 seconds plus 20% scroll, never on load. Always leave a 'teaser' tab after dismissal.
PREMIUM TWIST: discounts erode a premium price, so the offer is access and identity: 'Get early access and first pick of Founders serial numbers.'
EMERGING: trigger on engagement, not a timer. After a visitor turns the hero dial through 3 or more detent profiles, slide in: 'Liked that? Be first to feel the real one.' Step 1 is one tap: 'What will you turn it for? [Editing] [Music] [3D/Design] [Code] [Streaming]'. Step 2 is email. Step 3 (optional) is a referral link and queue position. The step-1 answer sets the email segment and routes the next page view to /for/<segment>.
findings.applyTo: <capture-sheet> web component (a native <dialog> with non-modal show(), respecting prefers-reduced-motion) listening for the dial's 'detent-profile-change' CustomEvent count of 3 or more. Teaser: a bottom-left pill 'Get early access'. The segment is stored in localStorage (wrapped in try/catch) and appended as ?seg= in the verify link.
findings.risk: Google demotes intrusive interstitials on mobile, so use a bottom sheet under 30% of viewport height, never a full-screen cover on first view. Show it at most once per session and suppress it for 30 days after dismissal.

findings.title: Replacing exit-intent popups: save the build, a calendar reminder for launch day, and a shareable configuration
findings.detail:
EMERGING BET. Exit-intent doesn't exist on mobile (no cursor leaving the window), and it interrupts. Baymard notes that 43% of abandoners were 'just browsing' and that users rely on save features (21% for comparison), yet 89% of sites make saving hard. Give leaving visitors a reason to come back that they choose themselves:
(1) 'Save this build': the configuration is kept in the URL and in localStorage, with an optional 'email me this build' (one field).
(2) 'Add launch to calendar': a downloadable .ics (VEVENT with a VALARM 15 minutes before) for the deposit-open and launch-day times from launch.ts. This is a zero-account commitment device that beats Web Push, which on iOS needs an installed PWA.
(3) 'Send to a friend or boss' via navigator.share({title, text, url}), with a generated OG card of their configured dial (finish plus serial).
(4) A persistent mini 'Your build' chip in the header so returning visitors resume where they left off.
findings.applyTo: <save-build> and <launch-reminder> components on /shop, /launch/*, and each /for/* page. A build-time Astro endpoint generates /launch.ics from launch.ts. Dynamic OG images come from a Worker route (Satori/resvg) at /og/build?finish=&serial=.
findings.risk: Put the date and time in the .ics in UTC with TZID and keep it in sync if the launch slips; publish it at a stable URL so calendar subscribers get updates. Web Share falls back to copy-link on desktop Firefox.

findings.title: Referral waitlist: queue position plus premium, non-monetary milestone rewards
findings.detail:
PROVEN mechanics: Robinhood reached about 1M pre-launch signups with nothing but a visible queue position and a share link. Harry's gathered about 100k emails in a week with tiered milestone rewards. Benchmarks: median referral rate 9-10%, strong above 18%.
DETENT DESIGN:
- The thank-you screen shows the position immediately: 'You're #4,812.' Each verified referral jumps you 250 places.
- Milestones reward identity and craft, not discounts:
  - 1 referral: an exclusive 'Referral Ratchet' haptic profile, unlocked in the web demo now and on the device later;
  - 3: first-wave deposit access (the 72-hour priority window);
  - 10: choose your Founders serial before the public;
  - 25: an engraved custom knob face.
- A public leaderboard shows handles only (opt-in).
- Count only verified referrals (double opt-in and a distinct email domain check) to stop gaming.
EMERGING: the referral reward is playable immediately in the browser's 3D dial, so the reward loop closes in seconds, not months.
findings.applyTo: /launch/waitlist thank-you state: a <queue-position> component with an animated counter (counter-rolling via CSS @property transition, respecting prefers-reduced-motion). The referral link is /r/<code>, which sets a cookie-free ?ref= param carried to signup. Unlocked profiles are stored in localStorage and in the profile library.
findings.risk: Fraud: throttle signups per IP and domain, and require verification before counting. Keep the rewards deliverable (engraving capacity), and don't promise money-equivalent rewards whose tax or legal status you haven't checked.

findings.title: Agentic commerce, part 1: complete schema.org JSON-LD (ProductGroup, Offer PreOrder, shipping, returns, certifications, and the 3D GLB)
findings.detail:
PROVEN and supported by Google today; also what AI shopping agents parse. AI-referred retail traffic grew 769% year over year in Nov 2025 and converted 31% better than other traffic (Adobe).
Emit on /shop:
- ProductGroup {productGroupID:'DT1', variesBy:['https://schema.org/color','https://schema.org/material'], hasVariant:[Product...]}.
- Each variant: {sku, gtin (once assigned), mpn, brand, image[], color, material:'6061-T6 aluminum', subjectOf:{'@type':'3DModel', encoding:{'@type':'MediaObject', contentUrl:'/models/detent-one.glb', encodingFormat:'model/gltf-binary'}}}. The same GLB the three.js hero loads doubles as Google-supported 3D model markup.
- hasCertification (FCC, CE, RoHS once real).
- Offer {price:'349.00', priceCurrency:'USD', availability:'https://schema.org/PreOrder' during the deposit phase ('InStock' at store phase), availabilityStarts:'<launch ISO date>', priceValidUntil, url with config params, shippingDetails:OfferShippingDetails {shippingRate, shippingDestination, deliveryTime {handlingTime, transitTime} in days}}.
- The Organization carries hasMerchantReturnPolicy: {applicableCountry:'US', returnPolicyCategory:'MerchantReturnFiniteReturnWindow', merchantReturnDays:100, returnMethod:'ReturnByMail', returnFees:'FreeReturn'}. Since the Nov 2025 update this is supported org-wide, and product level overrides it.
- The Founders Edition is its own Product with its own Offer, because 'edition' isn't a supported variesBy value.
- No aggregateRating until real reviews exist.
findings.applyTo: src/lib/schema.ts builds the JSON-LD from the same launch.ts and product data the UI uses (single source of truth), injected via <script type="application/ld+json"> in the Astro layout. Validate with Google's Rich Results Test and schema.org validator in CI (e.g. a structured-data-testing npm step).
findings.risk: Data drift between the JSON-LD and the visible page is a Merchant Center policy violation, so generate both from one source. PreOrder offers without a ship date or with a wrong price get disapproved. The GLB must be glTF for Google, and USDZ is separate for iOS AR.

findings.title: Agentic commerce, part 2: feeds and protocols. AI finds the product, the purchase happens on Detent's site, and agent handoff links carry the configuration
findings.detail:
STATE OF PLAY, September 2026:
- OpenAI launched ChatGPT Instant Checkout on ACP in Sept 2025, then retired it in March 2026. Fewer than 30 merchants went live, and Walmart measured in-chat checkout converting about 3x worse than a click-through to its own site, while ChatGPT brought about 2x the new-customer rate. The durable pattern is 'discover in AI, buy on your own site'.
- ACP (Apache 2.0, date-versioned, latest stable 2026-04-17, covering cart, feed, orders, auth and MCP) and OpenAI's product feed live on.
- Google's UCP (launched Jan 2026 at NRF; March 2026 added Cart, Catalog and Identity Linking plus Merchant Center onboarding) serves AI Mode and Gemini. Merchants publish a JSON manifest at /.well-known/ucp and support REST, MCP, A2A or AP2 transports.
- Perplexity with PayPal Instant Buy (Nov 2025) made more than 5,000 PayPal merchants discoverable.
- Payment networks are converging on Web Bot Auth (RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures): Visa Trusted Agent Protocol, Mastercard Agent Pay, Amex.
DETENT PLAN:
(1) Generate /feeds/openai.jsonl at build with OpenAI's required fields {item_id, title (150 chars or fewer), description (5,000 or fewer), url, brand, seller_name, image_url, availability:'pre_order', price:'349.00 USD'} plus availability_date, return_window:100, enable_search:true, enable_checkout:false.
(2) Generate /feeds/google.xml, a Merchant Center feed with the same data.
(3) Publish a /.well-known/ucp manifest declaring catalog, with checkout added later via the payments provider (Stripe is implementing UCP).
(4) The emerging bet: AGENT HANDOFF URLs. Every configuration is a deterministic, crawlable URL (/shop?finish=graphite&edition=founders), so an agent can hand the human a pre-configured page. The express-pay button is the only step left.
(5) Never block verified agents at the edge; allow signed Web Bot Auth agents when checkout moves behind Cloudflare.
findings.applyTo: Astro endpoints src/pages/feeds/openai.jsonl.ts, src/pages/feeds/google.xml.ts and src/pages/.well-known/ucp.json.ts (or a static file under public/.well-known/). If deploying from a branch instead of the withastro/action workflow, add public/.nojekyll so GitHub Pages serves the dot-directory. The /agents page documents the feeds for partners.
findings.risk: Protocols are still churning (ACP has had 5 versions in 7 months), so treat these as generated artifacts from one data source, not handwritten integrations. OpenAI feeds are pushed to an OpenAI endpoint after merchant approval; a static file alone doesn't enroll you. UCP checkout is limited to eligible US merchants. Don't enable in-agent checkout for a preorder or deposit flow.

findings.title: llms.txt and HTML parity: every fact in the 3D scenes also exists as plain HTML text; llms.txt only for the SDK docs
findings.detail:
EVIDENCE, 2026: llms.txt does nothing for search or AI citations.
- Google (June 2026): 'no effect, positive or negative' on Search or AI Overviews.
- A 300k-domain study found no correlation with citations.
- Server logs showed 0 fetches from GPTBot, ClaudeBot and the like on a 900-domain panel, and about 0.1% of AI-bot hits elsewhere.
The real consumers are coding agents and IDE assistants fetching docs on demand. Adoption is 69% among developer-tools sites. Detent has an open SDK and a developer audience, so ship /llms.txt: H1, a summary blockquote, H2 link lists of about 50 links or fewer to SDK quickstart, haptic profile schema, API reference, specs and policies. Add /llms-full.txt, a concatenated Markdown version of the SDK docs, so developers' agents write correct Detent profiles. Regenerate both at build.
More important for AI shoppers: WebGL canvas content is invisible to crawlers and agents. Every claim made in the three.js hero, the exploded view and the feel demo (torque, latency, detent counts, dimensions) must also exist as semantic HTML: <dl> spec lists, <table> comparisons, a question-shaped FAQ ('Does Detent One work with DaVinci Resolve?'). The /for/* and /integrations/* pages answer the long-tail questions agents ask.
findings.applyTo: src/pages/llms.txt.ts and llms-full.txt.ts generated from the SDK docs content collection; an optional mirror at /.well-known/llms.txt. Every three.js section wraps a <canvas aria-hidden> next to real HTML content (visually integrated, not display:none). FAQPage JSON-LD is optional because Google rich results for FAQ are restricted, but the HTML Q&A itself is what matters.
findings.risk: Low cost, low upside for commerce. Don't sell it internally as SEO. Keep it in sync with the docs or it misleads coding agents.

findings.title: Speed as a conversion feature: prerender the next page, cross-document View Transitions, and a still image (not WebGL) as the largest paint
findings.detail:
PROVEN: Ray-Ban's prerendering with the Speculation Rules API cut mobile LCP from 4.69s to 2.66s and lifted conversion 101% on mobile and 156% on desktop, with exits down 13%. Its bfcache work cut LCP 28% and CLS from 0.46 to 0.08. The rules: 'moderate' eagerness (hover) on desktop, and 'immediate' for the first 4 tiles on mobile. 35% of mobile sites used Speculation Rules by 2025.
IMPLEMENTATION for Astro:
- In astro.config set prefetch:{prefetchAll:false, defaultStrategy:'hover'} and experimental.clientPrerender:true (it uses Speculation Rules), or inline <script type="speculationrules">{"prerender":[{"where":{"href_matches":"/shop*"},"eagerness":"moderate"},{"where":{"selector_matches":"[data-cta=primary]"},"eagerness":"eager"}]}</script>.
- Cross-document View Transitions via @view-transition{navigation:auto;}, with view-transition-name:dial on the hero dial so it morphs from the homepage into /shop (Chromium and Safari 18.2+; others degrade gracefully).
- The LCP element is an AVIF poster of the dial (fetchpriority="high", with width and height set). Initialize three.js after the first input or in requestIdleCallback, with Draco/Meshopt-compressed GLB under 1.5 MB and KTX2 textures.
- Budgets: LCP 2.0s or less, INP 150ms or less, CLS 0.05 or less at p75 on a mid-tier Android over 4G, enforced by Lighthouse CI in GitHub Actions.
- Keep pages bfcache-eligible: no unload handlers, and close WebGL contexts on pagehide.
findings.applyTo: astro.config.mjs (prefetch, clientPrerender), the base layout head (speculationrules script, @view-transition CSS), the <dial-hero> component (poster first, dynamic import('three') after interaction or idle, and a matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)') path that keeps the static poster plus an HTML range input as the dial), and .github/workflows/lighthouse.yml with budgets.
