Email-walling the experience: requiring signup before someone can play with the dial. The toy is the top of the funnel and must be free and instant.
Client-side 'global leaderboards' presented as real. They can be spoofed trivially and there is nowhere to store them. Keep leaderboards personal-best or GitHub-backed (PR-merged), or leave them out.
Upvote begging, vote rings or new-account brigades on Product Hunt and Hacker News. Both detect and punish them, and PH now features only about 10% of launches.
Mandatory scroll-jacked 3D with no reduced-motion or keyboard path. It hurts accessibility and conversion and does nothing for Awwwards' developer and usability scores.
A random prize drawing or giveaway with no official rules, no free alternative entry, and no NY/FL registration when prizes exceed $5,000.
Autoplaying sound. Web Audio must start only after a user gesture, with a visible sound toggle.

lens: three.js / real-time 3D on production marketing sites (Sept 2026): the Detent One interactive dial hero. Covers renderer choice, loading, budgets, materials, procedural knob, display, physics, accessibility, resilience, and headless stills. Web research is combined with hands-on checks run on three r186.1, esbuild, and Playwright 1.63 / Chromium 153 on an Apple M4. Bundle sizes, headless timings, AVIF sizes and test renders were measured, not quoted.

findings.title: Renderer strategy: write against three/webgpu + TSL with the automatic WebGL2 fallback, keep it off the critical path, and keep a forceWebGL kill switch
findings.detail:
STATUS (verified): three latest is 0.186.1 on npm. r186 shipped 2026-09-08 on a roughly 8-11 week cadence. In the r186 source, `import { WebGPURenderer } from 'three/webgpu'` builds a WebGPUBackend with `getFallback: () => new WebGLBackend()`, and `forceWebGL: true` forces WebGL2. WebGPU is on by default in Chrome/Edge 113+ desktop, Chrome Android 121+ (Android 12+), Safari 26 (macOS, iOS, iPadOS, visionOS; webkit.org confirms), and Firefox 141 (Windows) / 145 (Apple Silicon). Firefox on Linux and Android is still pending. Global support is roughly 83-87%.

WHAT BREAKS: ShaderMaterial, RawShaderMaterial, onBeforeCompile, EffectComposer and pmndrs/postprocessing do not run on WebGPURenderer on either backend. Custom shading has to be TSL. r183 renamed PostProcessing to RenderPipeline (the old name is still exported) and deprecated Clock in favour of Timer. r186 removed PCFSoftShadowMap.

MEASURED (esbuild --minify, r186.1, the same knob scene: LatheGeometry + MeshPhysicalMaterial + PMREM/RoomEnvironment + CanvasTexture):
- WebGLRenderer: 547 KB raw / 137 KB gzip / 113 KB brotli
- WebGPURenderer: 957 KB / 247 KB gz / 200 KB br
- WebGPU + TSL + RenderPipeline + bloom: 1,072 KB / 280 KB gz / 225 KB br
- PR #34533 (merged 2026-09-17, r187) makes three/tsl tree-shakeable. It cut 12.4% gzipped in its own benchmark.

PERFORMANCE: in an 11-draw-call, ~5k-triangle scene, WebGPU brings no FPS gain. Issue #33821 (June 2026) measured material init 16-36x slower on WebGPURenderer when there are many materials. We have ~6 materials.

RECOMMENDATION: the long-term bet is three/webgpu + TSL, because that is where every new feature lands (RenderPipeline, TRAA/SSGI, compute, HDR canvas output, SunLight CSM). Load it only after LCP (see the loading finding), so the extra ~110 KB gz never competes with first paint.

IMPLEMENTATION:
- `const renderer = new WebGPURenderer({ antialias: tier >= 2, forceWebGL: cfg.forceWebGL || url.has('gl') }); await renderer.init();`
- Report `renderer.backend.isWebGPUBackend` to RUM. Do not use `isWebGPURenderer`, which is true on both backends.
- Use `renderer.setAnimationLoop` and `new Timer()`.

PROVEN FALLBACK: if the hero chunk must be at or under ~120 KB br, use WebGLRenderer with only built-in MeshPhysicalMaterial features (no GLSL patches). Migrating later is then a one-line import swap.
findings.applyTo: src/three/renderer.ts (factory returns {renderer, backend}). The launch-phase config gets `render.forceWebGL` and `render.backend: 'auto'|'webgl'`. Used by the hero island, /configure and /feel pages.
findings.risk: On the WebGL2 fallback, WebGPURenderer can be slower than WebGLRenderer, and its API still breaks every release or two (r183 and r185 had breaking changes). Pin an exact three version, read the release notes before bumping, and gate upgrades with golden-image tests (see the headless finding). Firefox Android users get the WebGL2 fallback.

findings.detail: A is never an LCP candidate (web.dev), so the hero should be a server-rendered of the exact scene and camera. Render it headlessly (see the headless finding). POSTER MARKUP: - `` inside a stage with `aspect-ratio: 1200/630` (no CLS). - MEASURED 1200x630 poster sizes: AVIF q50 15 KB, AVIF q62 20 KB, WebP q78 24 KB, mozjpeg q82 34 KB, PNG 185 KB. Show a real
findings.applyTo: Home hero island (DialHero.astro plus the web component <detent-hero>), /for/* audience heroes (the same module with different camera/colorway presets), and the launch pages (tease, waitlist, reserve, launch, store) that reuse the hero.
findings.risk: If the poster and live camera or tone mapping differ, the crossfade 'pops'. Generate the poster from the same module and config (see the headless finding). requestIdleCallback is missing in older Safari, so the setTimeout fallback is required. Don't lazy-load the poster.

findings.title: Hard performance budgets for the WebGL hero, enforced in CI and RUM
findings.detail:
Targets are stricter than CWV 'good' because the site sells a precision product.

FIELD TARGETS (p75, mobile):
- LCP ≤ 1.8 s (good is ≤ 2.5 s)
- INP ≤ 150 ms (good is ≤ 200 ms; INP counts only clicks, taps and key presses, not pointermove or scroll)
- CLS ≤ 0.02

CRITICAL PATH (before LCP):
- Zero bytes of three.js.
- HTML with inline critical CSS ≤ 30 KB br.
- Poster ≤ 25 KB at 1x and ≤ 60 KB at 2x (measured 15-20 KB AVIF at 1200 px).
- ≤ 2 WOFF2 subsets.

JS:
- Site shell (web components, nav, cart, Web Audio click synth) ≤ 30 KB br.
- 3D hero chunk ≤ 120 KB br on WebGL, or ≤ 210 KB br on the WebGPU path (measured 113 / 200 / 225 KB br).
- detect-gpu adds 3.4 KB gz.
- Configurator add-on ≤ 30 KB br.

3D ASSETS:
- 0 model downloads (procedural).
- Textures ≤ 50 KB total (the knurl normal map is 1.3-2.2 KB).
- No HDR/EXR files.
- VRAM ≤ 48 MB.

GPU:
- ≤ 20 draw calls (the knob measured 11) and ≤ 60k triangles.
- DPR capped per tier.
- While dragging, p90 frame time ≤ 12 ms on a mid-range Android.
- Zero frames rendered while idle.
- Poster-to-live swap ≤ 2.5 s after LCP with 4x CPU throttle and Fast 4G.
- No long task over 50 ms after the first interaction.

ENFORCEMENT:
- size-limit (or a bundle check) per chunk in CI.
- Lighthouse CI assertions on /, /reserve and /configure.
- A Playwright test scripts a 3 s drag and collects `PerformanceObserver({ type: 'long-animation-frame' })` (Chromium). It fails on any LoAF over 50 ms or a p90 over 12 ms.
- RUM uses the web-vitals attribution build, tagged with {backend, tier, dprCap}.

Awwwards jurors test on real mid-range Android with DevTools 4x CPU and Fast 3G, and sites that drop to ~18 fps do not place.
findings.applyTo: /.size-limit.json, lighthouserc.json, tests/perf/hero-drag.spec.ts, and src/lib/rum.ts. Budget numbers live next to the launch-phase config so every landing page inherits them.
findings.risk: M4 lab numbers (1.3-1.7 ms/frame at DPR 2) overstate mobile headroom by 5-10x. Validate on a physical Pixel 6a / Galaxy A-series class device before launch. LoAF is Chromium-only, so rely on RUM for Safari.

findings.title: Render on demand: an invalidate() loop that only runs while something moves, pauses off-screen, and drives the page through one CSS variable
findings.applyTo: src/three/loop.ts shared by hero, configurator and feel-profile demos. Page-level reactions (type weight, accent hue, section progress) read var(--dial) in CSS.
findings.risk: OrbitControls-style damping needs the loop to keep running until settled; the 'moving' flag must include spring residuals. Writing --dial on :root restyles the whole document, so scope it to the hero section, or check in DevTools that style recalc stays under 1 ms.

findings.title: Adaptive quality: detect-gpu as a coarse prior, a frame-time governor with hysteresis as ground truth, and explicit tiers
findings.detail:
DETECT-GPU (v5.0.70, verified in the package):
- Last published 2025-02-26, so its benchmark data predates recent GPUs (for example, its Apple list stops at A17).
- It reads WEBGL_debug_renderer_info, which it skips in Firefox. Safari reports only 'Apple GPU', so it guesses from a precision test.
- It fetches per-vendor JSON (0.2-13 KB gz) from unpkg by default. Self-host it: `getGPUTier({ benchmarksURL: '/gpu-bench', glContext })`, and pass the renderer's own GL context to avoid a second context.
- Default fps tiers are [0, 15, 30, 60].
- Use it only to choose the starting tier and the tier-0 poster-only case (WEBGL_UNSUPPORTED or BLOCKLISTED).

TIERS:
- T0: poster plus CSS affordance. Applies when there is no WebGL2, when `getContext('webgl2', { failIfMajorPerformanceCaveat: true })` fails, when Save-Data is on, or when detect-gpu reports tier 0.
- T1: DPR cap 1.0 on phones / 1.25 on desktop; antialias off; lathe segments 128; anisotropy 0 (roughness only); glass without clearcoat; halo instead of bloom.
- T2: DPR cap 1.5; MSAA (antialias: true, 4 samples); full materials; halo.
- T3: DPR cap 2.0; MSAA; selective display bloom (WebGPU); optional HDR display.

GOVERNOR:
- Sample frame time only while the loop is active (idle frames don't exist).
- Keep an EWMA over about 60 frames and compare against budget = 1000 / measured refresh (rAF deltas).
- Step down when p90 exceeds 1.25x budget for 2 s: first DPR -0.25 (not below 1), then bloom off, then MSAA off.
- Step up only after 5 s under 0.6x budget.
- After 2 direction flips, lock the tier (the drei PerformanceMonitor flipflops pattern). Persist it in sessionStorage.
- Avoid the naive sbcode approach (100 ms windows, ×0.9/×1.1 steps), which oscillates.

DPR: always `renderer.setPixelRatio(Math.min(devicePixelRatio, cap))`, and re-apply it on a `matchMedia(`(resolution: ${devicePixelRatio}dppx)`)` change (monitor swap).

EMERGING SIGNALS: WebGPU `adapter.info` (vendor, architecture, type: discrete/integrated) and `requestAdapter({ featureLevel: 'compatibility' })` (Chrome 146) can classify GPUs without the deprecated debug extension, but they still give no FPS number.
findings.applyTo: src/three/tier.ts runs before import('./hero3d') for the T0 decision. src/three/governor.ts runs inside the loop. The tier is exposed as data-tier on <html> for CSS.
findings.risk: Mid-drag DPR changes cause a resize flash, so only apply them on settle. Thermal throttling on phones appears after 30-60 s, so keep the governor on. Don't fingerprint: never send raw renderer strings to analytics, only the tier.

findings.title: Procedural machined knob: separate lathe parts, real-mm units, crisp chamfers, a static display with a rotating ring
findings.detail:
No GLB download is needed. Build the knob from profiles in meters (knob radius 0.018, height 0.024) so AR and USDZ exports are true to size; a camera near plane of 0.005 is fine.

PARTS (verified in test renders):
1. Top ring: `LatheGeometry(profile, 256)` from the display bezel out to the chamfer start. LatheGeometry UVs run u around the axis and v along the profile point index (not arc length), and with anisotropy that produces the radial 'spun' highlight of a turned face automatically.
2. Chamfers: 2-point lathe profiles at 45°, 0.4-0.6 mm (about 2-3% of radius). These catch the bright specular line that says 'machined'.
3. Knurled side: `CylinderGeometry(r, r, h, 256, 1, true)`, so it has its own UVs (u = circumference, v = height) for the knurl normal map.
4. Bottom chamfer.
5. Display disc plus glass disc: a separate, NON-rotating group. As in SmartKnob View's hollow shaft, the screen stays upright while the ring turns. In my test, parenting the display to the rotating ring turned the UI upside down.
6. Base: `CylinderGeometry(0.0241, 0.0248, 0.0054, 192)`, with a slight draft.
7. Tick ring decal.

NORMALS: never smooth-shade across 90° corners (that gives a pillowy, plastic look). Use separate meshes, or `toCreasedNormals(geometry, THREE.MathUtils.degToRad(30))` from BufferGeometryUtils so flats stay flat.

SEGMENTS: 256 around keeps the silhouette smooth at DPR 2 and a knob over 600 px wide (128 facets are visible). The full knob came to about 5k triangles.

LEGIBLE ROTATION: a rotationally symmetric knurl reads weakly while spinning, so add an engraved index dot or line on the top ring.

All parts share 3-4 materials, giving 11 draw calls in the test.
findings.applyTo: src/three/knob/geometry.ts (pure functions of a KnobSpec {diameterMm, heightMm, chamferMm, knurlPitchMm}). Reused by the hero, the configurator (Founders Edition variant: different chamfer and knurl), and the build-time exporters.
findings.risk: LatheGeometry v is not arc-length based, so don't map patterned textures on it; that is why the knurl sits on a separate cylinder. Very small world units are fine in fp32, but keep the camera near/far ratio ≤ 1:10,000.

findings.title: Premium aluminum without HDR files: MeshPhysicalMaterial anisotropy recipes, RoomEnvironment PMREM, and a bright environment (a dark one turns metal black)
findings.detail:
ENVIRONMENT:
- `const pmrem = new PMREMGenerator(renderer); scene.environment = pmrem.fromScene(env, 0.04).texture;` where env is RoomEnvironment, a tiny procedural scene with no network fetch.
- MEASURED A/B: a custom dark 'studio' (0.02 grey room plus thin emissive strips) rendered the silver knob as near-black gunmetal. RoomEnvironment gave bright, legible aluminum and crisp knurl. Metal only shows what it reflects.
- For signature highlights, `.add()` 1-2 extra emissive planes to the RoomEnvironment scene before fromScene, for example a thin horizontal strip with `MeshBasicMaterial({ color: new Color(20, 20, 20) })`. PMREM captures values above 1 as HDR.
- `scene.environmentIntensity` 0.9-1.2.
- For a cheap 'light sweep' on scroll or hover, animate `scene.environmentRotation.y`; it re-renders without regenerating the PMREM.

MATERIAL RECIPES (metalness 1 throughout):
- Spun top ring: color #d4d6da, roughness 0.28, anisotropy 0.9, anisotropyRotation 0.
- Diamond-cut chamfers: roughness 0.10-0.14, anisotropy 0.6.
- Knurled or bead-blasted side: roughness 0.36-0.40, anisotropy 0.5, plus the knurl normal map.
- Bead-blasted base: roughness 0.45-0.55, anisotropy 0. Optionally add a 256² noise roughnessMap of ±0.04 to break up uniformity.
- Space Black anodized: color #2a2c30, roughness 0.5.
- Colorways change only material.color and roughness, never textures.

ANISOTROPY in three r186: alphaT = mix(roughness², 1, anisotropy²). Direction is (cos, sin)(anisotropyRotation) in tangent space, and the tangent frame comes from UV derivatives. An anisotropyMap uses RG as the direction (×2−1) and B as strength, with NoColorSpace.

GLASS over the display: `MeshPhysicalMaterial({ color: 0x000000, roughness: 0.02, transparent: true, opacity: 0.25, clearcoat: 1, clearcoatRoughness: 0, ior: 1.52 })` gives a convincing 'under glass' sheen. Do NOT use transmission, which adds a full extra scene pass.

The scene needs no punctual lights; IBL only.
findings.applyTo: src/three/knob/materials.ts (a recipe table keyed by colorway and finish) and src/three/env.ts (RoomEnvironment plus brand strips, regenerated after context restore). The /configure colorway picker changes uniforms only.
findings.risk: Anisotropy and clearcoat add shader cost. Turn anisotropy off on T1. The PMREM is a render target, so its contents are lost on WebGL context loss (see the context-loss finding). An environment that is too uniform makes the knurl read as noise; the extra strips fix that.

findings.title: Color management and tone mapping: Khronos PBR Neutral for product truth, toneMapped:false for UI pixels, strict texture color spaces
findings.detail:
TONE MAPPING:
- `renderer.toneMapping = NeutralToneMapping; renderer.toneMappingExposure = 1.0`. Khronos PBR Neutral (May 2024) was designed for e-commerce and CAD color fidelity and is adopted by three.js, model-viewer, Babylon and Blender. It keeps anodized hues true, so the configurator matches photos and the checkout.
- AgXToneMapping is acceptable for a moodier hero. In my A/B it lifted the floor and greys and desaturated highlights.
- Avoid ACESFilmic for products; it shifts saturated oranges.

UI PIXELS: set `toneMapped: false` on the display material, the halo, and any brand-colored mesh so the #FF5A1F-style accent matches CSS exactly under any tone mapper. On the WebGPU RenderPipeline, keep tone mapping in the final renderOutput so post effects don't double-apply it.

COLOR SPACES:
- Color textures (display CanvasTexture, tick-ring canvas): `SRGBColorSpace`.
- Normal, roughness and anisotropy maps: NoColorSpace (the default).
- Output stays SRGBColorSpace. Hex colors in code are sRGB, and ColorManagement converts them.

EMERGING: Display P3 output via `three/addons/math/ColorSpaces.js` (`DisplayP3ColorSpace` plus `ColorManagement.define`) lets saturated anodized colorways use wide gamut. Enable only when `matchMedia('(color-gamut: p3)')` matches, and keep sRGB posters.
findings.applyTo: src/three/renderer.ts defaults. Material factories enforce colorSpace on assignment (a lint/test asserting every .map has SRGBColorSpace and every data map has NoColorSpace).
findings.risk: Changing the tone mapper after the posters are generated creates a visible shift at the crossfade. Lock it in config and regenerate the stills in CI. P3 output needs checking on non-P3 screens (clipping).

findings.title: Knurling and engraved ticks: a 1-2 KB normal map (or a zero-byte TSL version with frequency clamping), plus a canvas tick ring
findings.applyTo: scripts/gen-knurl.mjs writes public/tex/knurl-128x64.png. src/three/knob/details.ts builds ticks with the same tick count as the active feel profile (12-click clock gets 12 ticks, etc.), so the base literally shows the detent layout.
findings.risk: bumpMap relies on screen-space derivatives and shimmers without the fwidth fade. With too high a normalScale, the knurl reads as noise at hero size; tune it on a real phone. Canvas tick rings rebuilt per profile cost a texture upload, which is fine because it happens only on a profile change.

findings.title: Round display in the knob face: a 480² CanvasTexture updated only on state change, fonts loaded first, one shared draw function
findings.detail:
PANEL: the product's 1.28" round panel is a GC9A01-class 240×240 LCD. Author the UI at 480×480 (2x) in a 2D canvas (OffscreenCanvas where available).

TEXTURE SETTINGS:
- `const tex = new CanvasTexture(cv); tex.colorSpace = SRGBColorSpace; tex.generateMipmaps = false; tex.minFilter = LinearFilter; tex.anisotropy = 8;`. Skipping mips avoids regenerating them on every update, and anisotropy keeps the oblique hero angle sharp.
- Material: `MeshBasicMaterial({ map: tex, toneMapped: false })` on a `CircleGeometry(r, 128)`. The disc UVs give the round mask for free, with no alpha.

UPDATES:
- Set `tex.needsUpdate = true` only when state changes: a detent is crossed, the profile switches, or an arc tween is running.
- MEASURED: the full frame at DPR 2 including a 480² upload was 1.3-1.7 ms on an M4, so the upload is negligible. Still, don't upload on idle frames.

FONTS: `await document.fonts.load('600 132px "Brand Display"')` before the first draw. Otherwise the fallback font is baked into the texture and into the Playwright stills.

SHARED DRAW FUNCTION: write one pure `drawDisplay(ctx, state, profile)`. It is reused by the 3D hero, the feel-library cards (plain 2D canvas, no WebGL), the configurator, and the OG/poster generator, so the brand renders pixel-identically everywhere.

Keep the display group static while the ring rotates (see the geometry finding).

RENDER TARGET: use one only if the display must show 3D content, because it costs an extra pass per update.

EMERGING: the HTML-in-Canvas API (`<canvas layoutsubtree>`, `gl.texElementImage2D`, `copyElementImageToTexture` for WebGPU, a paint event, `requestPaint()`) is in Chrome origin trial 148-150. It would make the display real, accessible, find-in-page-able DOM. No Firefox or Safari signal yet, so treat it as feature-detected progressive enhancement only (`'texElementImage2D' in gl`).
findings.applyTo: src/display/drawDisplay.ts (framework-free), src/three/knob/display.ts (the texture wrapper), and /feel/[profile] pages that render the same function without 3D.
findings.risk: CanvasTexture uploads stall more in Firefox and Safari at large sizes, so stay at 480² and don't go to 1024². Canvas text isn't accessible, so mirror the value in DOM (aria-valuetext and visible page copy).

findings.title: Soft contact shadow baked once (the dial only spins about Y); bloom only on the display, faked with a halo below T3
findings.detail:
CONTACT SHADOW: the dial's shadow and AO are rotation-invariant, so live contact shadows would waste 3-4 passes per frame. Options:
- (a) A 256² radial-gradient CanvasTexture on a plane under the base and under the knob. Zero download, used in my test renders.
- (b) Run the three.js contact-shadow technique ONCE at init and keep the result: orthographic camera of height 0.3 over a 2.5×2.5 plane, 512² render target, a depth material outputting (1 − z)·darkness, then horizontal plus vertical blur (blur ≈ 3.5, a second pass at 0.4×). Re-bake after context restore.
- (c) Bake it into a PNG in the headless pipeline.

No shadow maps and no punctual lights. If you add a sun later, note that r186 removed PCFSoftShadowMap; use PCFShadowMap.

BLOOM: only the display may glow.
- On T3 with WebGPU, use selective emissive bloom via MRT, per the official example: `const sp = pass(scene, cam); sp.setMRT(mrt({ output, emissive: vec4(emissive, output.a) })); const e = sp.getTextureNode('emissive'); pipeline.outputNode = sp.getTextureNode('output').add(bloom(e, 0.5, 0.3));`. Strength 0.4-0.8, radius 0.2-0.4. Set the emissive texture type to UnsignedByteType to save bandwidth.
- Elsewhere, use an additive camera-facing halo (a radial-gradient sprite, toneMapped false, opacity tied to display brightness). It costs about 0 ms and keeps native MSAA.
- A full-screen mip-chain bloom costs roughly 1-3 ms on mid-range mobile GPUs and forces an offscreen render target.

Never stack DOF, grain or chromatic aberration on a product hero; jurors reward restraint.
findings.applyTo: src/three/knob/shadow.ts (bake once, cache the texture) and src/three/post.ts (tier 3 plus WebGPU only; otherwise halo.ts).
findings.risk: A baked shadow breaks if you later animate the knob lifting or tilting (for example, an exploded view). Switch to a one-shot re-bake per keyframe, not per frame. The MRT bloom path is WebGPURenderer-only; WebGL needs a different implementation, so the halo is the portable default.

findings.title: Dial physics: port SmartKnob's detent model so the website and firmware share one feel-profile JSON, with pseudo-haptic drag coupling and inertia
findings.detail:
Mirror the device's config schema. SmartKnobConfig has position_width_radians, detent_strength_unit (0-1), endstop_strength_unit, snap_point (hysteresis, normally 1.1; 0.55 for on/off), snap_point_bias, min/max_position (max < min means unbounded), and detent_positions (up to 5 magnetic detents). One JSON then drives the web demo, the feel library, the SDK docs and the device.

FIRMWARE PRESETS to seed from:
- Unbounded: w = 10°, detents 0.
- On/off: w = 60°, s = 1, snap 0.55.
- Return-to-center: w = 60°, s = 0.01, endstop 0.6.
- Fine values: w = 1°, 0-255.
- Add a 12-click clock at w = 30°.

SIMULATION (fixed dt = 1/240 s):
- Let c be the detent center. If θ − c > w·snap, then c += w and position++, and fire onDetent; the same applies in the other direction.
- Restoring acceleration: −K·s_d·(θ − c) with the firmware dead zone, clamped to ±min(0.2·w, 1°) (DEAD_ZONE_DETENT_PERCENT = 0.2, DEAD_ZONE_RAD = 1°).
- Out of bounds, use K_e = 4·K·s_e (the firmware's P = strength·4) and fire onEdge.
- Visual tuning: ω_n ≈ 2π·8 Hz, so K ≈ 2,500 s⁻². Damping c = 2ζω_n, with ζ = 0.55 for a crisp micro-overshoot 'click' and ζ = 1 for fluid profiles.

PSEUDO-HAPTICS:
- Never set θ equal to the pointer angle. Couple them with a spring: α += K_c·(θ_ptr − θ) − C_c·ω, with K_c ≈ 5,000 s⁻².
- The knob then visibly lags and 'catches' at each ridge, and users perceive resistance (the visual-haptics effect).
- Compute pointer angle with atan2 around the knob's projected screen center (`center.clone().project(cam)`), and unwrap deltas to (−π, π].

INPUT AND INERTIA:
- Call `setPointerCapture(e.pointerId)`, and use `e.getCoalescedEvents?.()` for high-rate input.
- On release, take ω from a linear fit over the last 80 ms of samples, clamp |ω| ≤ 25 rad/s, and apply free-spin friction ω *= exp(−dt/0.4). The detent springs keep acting, so it naturally ratchets to a stop.
- The loop sleeps when |ω| < 0.02 and |θ − c| < 0.002.

ONDETENT FEEDBACK:
- Web Audio click, a display redraw and an aria update (throttled).
- `navigator.vibrate?.(8)`, which works on Chromium Android only; rate-limit it to 25/s and only after user activation.
- EMERGING: the WICG/Edge Web Haptics API explainer defines semantic effects tick, edge, align and hint (plus a CSS `haptic-feedback` property) that map 1:1 to detent, endstop and snap. Feature-detect and adopt when it ships.
findings.applyTo: packages/feel-core (TS, no DOM) holds the profile schema and physics step and is shared by the site and the SDK docs. src/three/knob/interaction.ts is the pointer layer. Feel-library pages load the same profiles.
findings.risk: Safari has no Vibration API. The iOS checkbox-switch haptic trick is reported patched in iOS 26.5, so don't ship it. Semi-implicit Euler at 240 Hz is stable for these stiffnesses; if you raise K much higher, lower dt or clamp. Too much lag from K_c feels broken on fast flicks, so raise K_c with speed.

findings.title: Scroll-safe touch: a knob-sized DOM hit target with touch-action:none, the rest of the hero pan-y, plus a non-drag alternative (WCAG 2.5.7)
findings.detail:
A full-viewport canvas with touch-action:none blocks page scroll on phones, which is a conversion killer. touch-action is decided before JS runs, so place a transparent circular element (`border-radius: 50%`) exactly over the knob's projected screen circle. Reposition it on resize and camera change. Give it `touch-action: none` and pointer handlers; the canvas and the rest of the stage keep `touch-action: pan-y` and `pointer-events: none` on the canvas. The same element is the accessible control (see the accessibility finding), so hit target, focus ring and ARIA are one node.

WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (AA) requires a single-pointer alternative to dragging:
- Visible −/+ step buttons (≥ 24×24 CSS px per SC 2.5.8; aim for 44 px).
- Tapping the left or right half of the knob steps one detent.
- Tapping a tick on the base jumps there.

Also add a small 'Try: flick it' hint that disappears after the first interaction.

Desktop: add a wheel handler on the knob (one detent per notch, with `{ passive: false }` only on the knob element) so trackpad users can scrub. Never hijack wheel events on the page.
findings.applyTo: <detent-knob-control> web component overlaid on the hero, configurator and feel pages. The position is synced from the three.js projection in the render loop, only when the camera moves.
findings.risk: The overlay drifts from the render if it is updated on a different frame than the render, so write both in the same tick. On iOS, preventDefault on touchmove must be on a non-passive listener attached to the hit element only.

findings.title: Canvas accessibility: a native range (or role=slider / role=spinbutton) is the real control, the canvas is decoration, and announcements are throttled
findings.detail:
Mark the canvas `aria-hidden="true"`; the poster img keeps a descriptive alt until it is hidden.

CONTROL:
- Bounded profiles: a visually hidden native `<input type=range min max step=1>` (clip pattern, not display:none) inside the knob hit element. It gives keyboard, iOS VoiceOver swipe-to-adjust and Android TalkBack support for free, and is more robust than a custom role=slider div.
- Unbounded jog/scroll profiles (max < min): a range needs bounds, so use `role="spinbutton"` with aria-valuenow and aria-valuetext and no min/max.

LABELS:
- `aria-label="Detent One dial, Timeline profile"`.
- aria-valuetext in human terms, for example 'Frame 42 of 240', '3 o'clock, 3 of 12', 'Volume 60 percent, end stop'.

KEYS (APG slider): arrows ±1 detent, PageUp/PageDown ±10% or ±5 detents, Home/End to min/max, plus Space/Enter to toggle on/off profiles.

FOCUS: draw a visible focus ring on the overlay circle via `:focus-visible` (or `:has(input:focus-visible)`), at 3:1 contrast against both the knob and the background.

THROTTLING:
- For pointer and flick input, update aria-valuenow/valuetext at most about 4 Hz and on settle, because a flick can cross 50 detents per second and would flood the screen reader.
- For keyboard input, update immediately on every step.

COMPANION TEXT: mirror the dial state in visible DOM (the page's reaction copy), so no information lives only in canvas pixels.
findings.applyTo: <detent-knob-control> (the same element as the touch hit target). Audience landing pages pass a profile whose valuetext formatter is domain-specific (frames for editors, BPM for producers).
findings.risk: A native range has its own pointer behavior. Keep it visually hidden with pointer-events:none and route pointer input through the overlay's physics, while the input handles keyboard and AT. Test with VoiceOver on iOS 26 and NVDA/JAWS. Don't set aria-roledescription unless AT testing shows it helps.

findings.title: prefers-reduced-motion and WCAG 2.2.2: keep direct manipulation, remove everything autonomous
findings.detail:
Read `const rm = matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)')` and listen for its 'change' event (users toggle it at runtime).

UNDER REDUCE:
- No idle 'attract' spin.
- No camera drift, parallax or scroll-driven camera.
- No flick inertia: release settles to the nearest detent critically damped within ≤ 120 ms.
- No bloom or halo pulsing.
- Poster-to-canvas swap is instant.
- Scroll-linked environmentRotation sweeps are off.

KEEP: 1:1 direct manipulation and detent snaps. The user initiates that motion, and the product IS the motion.

WITHOUT reduce: any autonomous motion (attract spin, light sweep) must stop within 5 s or have a visible pause control (WCAG 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide).

STILL IMAGE: the reduced-motion and T0 experience is the poster plus the non-drag controls, which is also the no-JS experience.

Jurors treat a missing reduced-motion path as a craft failure.
findings.applyTo: src/lib/motion.ts exports a reactive `reducedMotion` signal consumed by physics (inertia on/off), loop (attract), camera and CSS (@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)).
findings.risk: Don't disable the whole 3D view under reduced motion. Users with vestibular disorders can still want to turn the dial. Test the OS toggle at runtime in both directions.

findings.title: Context and device loss: regenerate render targets on WebGL restore, rebuild on WebGPURenderer loss, fall back to the poster, one context per page
findings.detail:
WebGLRenderer (verified in the r186 source):
- It listens to webglcontextlost (with preventDefault) and, on webglcontextrestored, calls initGLContext().
- Meshes, CanvasTextures and DataTextures re-upload lazily because their JS sources persist.
- Render-target CONTENTS do not come back: the PMREM from fromScene and any baked shadow render target.
- So: `canvas.addEventListener('webglcontextrestored', () => { scene.environment = pmrem.fromScene(env, 0.04).texture; rebakeShadow(); invalidate(); })`.

WebGPURenderer (verified in r186):
- `renderer.onDeviceLost = info => {...}` fires on BOTH backends. The WebGL2 backend forwards webglcontextlost with info.api 'WebGL'.
- The WebGL2 backend has NO restore path. The WebGPU backend can re-init (`await renderer.init()`), but you must rebuild the resources.

UNIFIED STRATEGY on loss:
1. Crossfade back to the poster (it is still in the DOM).
2. `renderer.dispose()` and drop references.
3. On the next visibilitychange to visible, or on user intent, rebuild the renderer, canvas and scene from app state (profile, value, colorway).
4. Allow at most 2 rebuilds per session, then stay on the poster, and log the reason to RUM.

PREVENTION:
- Use ONE WebGL/WebGPU context per page. Share a renderer between hero and configurator (move the canvas, or use setScissor/setViewport). Browsers cap active contexts (about 16 in Chrome) and iOS reclaims background ones.
- With Astro's ClientRouter, `transition:persist` on the hero island keeps the same context across page navigations instead of churning it.

TESTING: `renderer.forceContextLoss()` / `WEBGL_lose_context.loseContext()`, and Chrome `about:gpucrash` for WebGPU. Add a Playwright test that forces loss and asserts the poster is visible with no uncaught errors.
findings.applyTo: src/three/resilience.ts wraps the renderer factory. The launch config gets `render.maxRebuilds`. Add a tests/e2e/context-loss.spec.ts.
findings.risk: The forum claim that three.js 'automatically handles restore via renderer.debug.checkShaderErrors' is wrong. That flag only toggles shader error checks. Render targets must be regenerated manually. Don't rebuild in a tight loop on a crashing GPU.

findings.title: Headless product stills with Playwright: posters, OG images, cutouts and golden tests from the same scene code
findings.detail:
PIPELINE: after `astro build`, a script serves dist/ and opens a noindex route `/_render?shot=hero&colorway=silver&w=1200&h=630&dpr=2`.
- The route imports the same hero module with `{ forceWebGL: true, preserveDrawingBuffer: true, animate: false }`.
- It awaits `document.fonts.ready`, then `renderer.compileAsync`, then 2 rAFs, then sets `window.__ready = true`.
- Playwright waits for `waitForFunction(() => window.__ready)`, then calls `page.screenshot({ omitBackground: true })`.

MEASURED (Playwright 1.63, Chromium 153, Apple M4):
- Default `chromium.launch()` (headless shell) renders WebGL via SwiftShader. Playwright adds `--enable-unsafe-swiftshader` itself (verified in playwright-core), so it works on GPU-less GitHub runners even after Chrome removed the automatic SwiftShader fallback.
- In the headless shell, WebGPURenderer fell back to WebGL2 automatically.
- `chromium.launch({ channel: 'chromium' })` (new headless) used the real GPU (ANGLE Metal) and gave a working WebGPU backend.
- Per-shot time to first frame: 1.1-1.8 s on SwiftShader, 0.1-1.7 s on GPU (cold vs warm shader cache).
- WebGL2-fallback and WebGPU-backend renders matched visually, so use forceWebGL for deterministic stills.

OUTPUTS (via sharp):
- Posters as AVIF (q50-62, effort 6) plus WebP plus JPEG at 1x/2x, per colorway and per /for/* audience framing. Measured 15-20 KB AVIF at 1200×630.
- OG and Twitter cards as 1200×630 JPEG or PNG (don't rely on AVIF or WebP for scrapers). Keep them small (≈ ≤ 300 KB is commonly cited for WhatsApp).
- Transparent PNG cutouts for configurator swatches and email.
- Per-launch-phase OG variants: tease (silhouette), reserve, launch.

GOLDEN TESTS: pixelmatch with threshold 0.1, allowing ≤ 0.5% differing pixels, on 4-6 canonical shots, run on every three.js bump.

The poster is also the complete no-JS and T0 experience, so pair it with server-rendered specs and the price.
findings.applyTo: scripts/render-stills.mjs plus the src/pages/_render.astro route (excluded from the sitemap, with noindex). A GitHub Actions job runs after build and before deploy to Pages. Commit the outputs to dist/og/ and dist/posters/.
findings.risk: SwiftShader vs GPU produces small pixel differences, so generate goldens on the same runner type they are compared on. Canvas fonts must be loaded first. Headless WebGPU is not available on standard CI runners, so don't make stills depend on it.

findings.title: 'See it on your desk': export the procedural knob to GLB/USDZ at build time for iOS Quick Look and Android AR
findings.detail: A physical desk product converts better when buyers see its real size. The knob is authored in meters, so export it at build time: - `GLTFExporter` produces GLB for Android Scene Viewer / WebXR. - `USDZExporter` produces USDZ for iOS Quick Look. Both ship in r186 examples/jsm/exporters. - Both run in the same Playwright render route (then download the blob) or in Node with a DOM shim. MARKUP: ``. iOS expects the anchor's child to be an image to show the AR badge. Offer it only when `document.createElement('a').relList.supports('ar')` or on Android with an intent link. CAVEATS: - USD Preview Surface has no anisotropy. The exporter carries normal, emissive and clearcoat maps, so bake the brushed look into roughness variation. - Bake a static display frame into the emissiveMap. - Budget ≤ 300 KB per colorway at 128 segments. This is an emerging bet that is likely to grow over the next decade as WebXR and visionOS mature. It costs nothing at runtime, because the files are static assets linked from the configurator.
findings.applyTo: /configure and /store product pages, with a 'View on your desk' button next to the price. Exports are generated per colorway in scripts/export-ar.mjs.
findings.risk: Quick Look strips custom shading, so check the look on a real device. Keep the files out of the critical path (plain links only). Android intent URLs need the GLB served with the correct MIME type (model/gltf-binary). Configure that in the GitHub Pages build.

findings.title: Emerging bet: an HDR/EDR 'real OLED' glow for the round display via the WebGPU extended canvas, gated and display-only
findings.detail:
three r186's WebGPU backend configures the canvas with `toneMapping: { mode: 'extended' }` when the renderer uses `outputType: HalfFloatType` (verified in WebGPUBackend.js).

SETUP (the official webgpu_hdr example):
- `new WebGPURenderer({ antialias: true, outputType: HalfFloatType })`
- `ColorManagement.define({ [ExtendedSRGBColorSpace]: ExtendedSRGBColorSpaceImpl })` (from three/addons/math/ColorSpaces.js)
- `renderer.outputColorSpace = ExtendedSRGBColorSpace`
- Gate on `matchMedia('(dynamic-range: high)').matches && renderer.backend.isWebGPUBackend && tier === 3`.

USE: tone mappers compress everything to 0-1, so only toneMapped:false materials exceed SDR white. That is exactly the display. Drive its emissive to about 2-3x on HDR screens, and the knob's screen glows brighter than the page's white on MacBook XDR, iPhone and HDR monitors, like a real emissive panel. The aluminum stays tone-mapped SDR.

WHY IT WINS OVER THE DECADE: HDR panels are becoming the default on premium laptops and phones, and almost no marketing site uses web HDR yet, so it is a genuine 'how is that so bright?' moment that screenshots can't capture.
findings.applyTo: src/three/hdr.ts, an optional enhancement in the tier-3 path on the hero and /feel pages only. Controlled by launch config `render.hdrDisplay: true`.
findings.risk: WebGPU-only, with uneven browser and OS support. Screenshots and posters are SDR, so the swap may look brighter. Cap the peak to avoid eye strain in dark rooms. Test Safari 26 and Chrome separately, and keep a kill switch.

antiPatterns: A full-viewport canvas with touch-action:none (or preventDefault on touchmove). It blocks page scroll on phones and kills conversion.
Rendering continuously with an rAF loop while nothing moves. Idle frames drain batteries and spin up the fans on jurors' laptops.
Putting three.js or any 3D bytes on the critical path, or treating the canvas as the hero content. A canvas is never an LCP candidate, so ship a pixel-matched AVIF poster first.
Showing a '0-100% loading' screen or spinner for a procedural scene that has nothing to download.
Downloading 2-8 MB HDR/EXR environment maps when a RoomEnvironment PMREM does the job with zero bytes.
Using a dark environment for aluminum. Metal only reflects what is around it, and in the test the silver knob rendered near-black.
Using ACESFilmic (or no tone-mapping policy) for a product with brand colorways. Use Khronos PBR Neutral, and set toneMapped:false for UI and display pixels.
Writing ShaderMaterial, RawShaderMaterial or onBeforeCompile hacks. They lock you out of WebGPURenderer, where all new three.js features land.
Using EffectComposer or pmndrs/postprocessing with stacked bloom, DOF, grain and chromatic aberration on a product hero. It costs 3-10 ms a frame on mobile and cheapens the look.
Setting setPixelRatio(window.devicePixelRatio) with no cap. DPR 3 phones then render 9x the pixels of DPR 1.
Running live contact shadows or shadow maps for an object that only spins about its own axis. Bake them once.
Parenting the display to the rotating knob, or setting knob angle equal to pointer angle with no spring coupling. The first turns the UI upside down; the second loses the detent 'feel'.
Canvas-only information, an unlabeled canvas, or a role=img with no operable control. Missing keyboard support, missing aria-valuetext, and speech floods during flicks all fail accessibility.
Having no non-drag alternative for the dial (fails WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.7), or autonomous spins with no pause control (fails 2.2.2).
Relying on navigator.vibrate on iOS (unsupported) or the iOS checkbox-switch haptic hack (reported patched in iOS 26.5).
Fetching runtime dependencies from third-party CDNs, such as detect-gpu's default unpkg benchmarks or remote decoders. Self-host everything on GitHub Pages.

Using the deprecated APIs Clock (use Timer) and PostProcessing (now RenderPipeline), and removed ones like PCFSoftShadowMap. Also, upgrading three without golden-image tests, since breaking changes land every 1-2 releases.
Assuming three.js automatically restores the PMREM and render targets after WebGL context loss. It doesn't, and WebGPURenderer's WebGL2 backend has no restore path at all.
Generating OG images by hand, or letting stills drift from the live scene. Render them in CI from the same module and config with Playwright.
